Moving the Universal Cake tools from AGPL-3.0-or-later to GPL-2.0 would make them easier for cautious organizations to adopt, but it would remove the protection that matters most for a hosted radar: the right of network users to get the source. GPL-2.0 also lacks an explicit patent grant, is not compatible with Apache-2.0 code, and breaks the CC BY-SA 4.0 bridge that runs only to GPLv3.

The draft conclusion is to keep AGPL-3.0-or-later for anything run as a service, and to consider GPL-3.0-or-later, not GPL-2.0, for tools that are only ever distributed and run locally. This stays provisional until the licensing owner confirms it.

## What would change

The biggest difference is the network clause; most of the others follow from GPLv3 being written 16 years after GPLv2.

| Term                                                         | AGPL-3.0-or-later (current)   | GPL-2.0-only           | GPL-2.0-or-later        |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------- | ---------------------- | ----------------------- |
| Published                                                    | 2007                          | 1991                   | 1991                    |
| Source owed to network users of a modified version           | Yes, section 13               | No                     | No                      |
| Source owed when copies are distributed                      | Yes                           | Yes                    | Yes                     |
| Explicit patent licence from contributors                    | Yes                           | No, implied at best    | No, implied at best     |
| Anti-tivoization (installation information for consumer devices) | Yes                           | No                     | No                      |
| Cure period after a violation                                | Yes, 30 and 60 day provisions | No, rights end at once | No, rights end at once  |
| Can move to a future licence version                         | Yes                           | No                     | Yes, to GPLv3 and later |
| Combinable with GPLv3 or AGPLv3 code                         | Yes                           | No                     | Yes, by choosing v3     |
| Combinable with Apache-2.0 code                              | Yes                           | No, in the FSF's view  | Yes, by choosing v3     |

## Advantages of GPL-2.0

The case for GPL-2.0 is mostly about adoption and simplicity, not stronger protection.

- Fewer policy blocks. Many companies and some public bodies ban AGPL code outright but allow GPL-2.0, so procurement and IT reviews get shorter.
- Lighter duties for clients who host. A municipality or NGO that modifies a tool and runs it internally or on a public site would owe source only if it distributed copies, not to every visitor.
- Familiarity. GPL-2.0 is the licence of the Linux kernel and has decades of case history and community practice behind it.
- Shorter text. GPL-2.0 is about half the length of AGPLv3 and easier to explain to a non-specialist client.
- Fixed terms (GPL-2.0-only). No future licence version can change what contributors agreed to, which is the reason Linus Torvalds keeps the kernel on version 2 only.
- Kernel and embedded alignment. Code that might one day be shared with GPL-2.0-only projects, such as kernel modules or some embedded firmware, can be combined directly.

## Disadvantages of GPL-2.0

The main cost is that a hosted fork could stay closed, which is the exact risk the AGPL was chosen to prevent.

- The network gap. A vendor or consultancy could modify `uc-radar`, run it as a paid rating service and never publish its changes. GPL-2.0 is triggered by distributing copies, not by serving users.
- No explicit patent grant. Contributors do not expressly licence their patents, and there is no patent retaliation clause, so downstream users of a tool have weaker protection.
- Harsh termination. Any violation ends a licensee's rights immediately, with no cure period, which is a poor fit for small organizations that make honest mistakes.
- No anti-tivoization. A device maker could ship a modified tool on locked hardware that users cannot update, which works against agency and longevity.
- Compatibility losses. GPL-2.0-only cannot be combined with GPLv3, AGPLv3 or Apache-2.0 code, which rules out a large share of modern libraries (Apache Software Foundation, n.d.).
- Dated wording. GPLv2 was written around US concepts like "distribution"; GPLv3 uses "convey" and "propagate" to work more evenly across jurisdictions, including Canada.
- Mixed signals. A practice that scores vendors on sovereignty would be choosing a weaker copyleft for its own hosted tools.

content.content: /home/initial/areas/buisness-ideas: total 4 -rw-rw-r-- 1 initial initial 47 Oct 19 01:21 httpswww.facebook.comreel28036421662727524.md /home/initial/areas/saas: total 16 -rw-rw-r-- 1 initial initial 8416 Oct 15 17:25 how-much-does-the-city-of-montreal-spend-on-saas.md -rw-rw-r-- 1 initial initial 3115 Oct 15 17:20 canada-software-as-a-service-saas-market-highlights.md /home/initial/areas/clients: total 4 drwxrwxr-x 2 initial initial 4096 Oct 15 16:22 francois --- title: "Creating the Initial osat-manager-git: Process Overview" description: "How the initial osat-manager-git was scoped and planned: from feasibility to a unified git base, Universal Cake requirements, and a proposed build sequence." identifier: "urn:uuid:90391798-a7d9-4f30-b7c1-bd9e40bba160" language: "en-ca" creator: "Christopher Steel" date: "2026-09-30" version: "0.1.0" status: "provisional" relation: "https://github.com/steelcj/uc-radar" --- # Creating the Initial osat-manager-git: Process Overview osat-manager-git is being built first as a unified git base: it manages multiple git installations on Linux, macOS and Windows through the standard osat CLI, with translated messages, so that every other osat manager can rely on git being present and correct. This overview records how that decision was reached and how the work proceeds. It is a provisional draft, drafted with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic), and stays provisional until Christopher Steel confirms it. ## Where this fits The long-term goal is highly accessible, safe, secure and multilingual applications, measured against the Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics (Steel, n.d.). One example is a very user-friendly, git-backed interface for managing SAT content, where a person adds a document, gives it a good title and description, and never needs to learn git. That interface depends on git working the same way everywhere. osat-manager-git provides that foundation, and building it is also the first chance to turn the Universal Cake metrics into concrete, testable requirements. ## Step one: confirm feasibility Two meanings of "managing git" were considered: managing git itself, and managing repositories inside a SAT hierarchy. Both are feasible. Managing git itself came first, because the repository work depends on it and because the SAT config cascade specification is still being written. ## Step two: define a baseline contract, not an install method The central idea is a baseline contract that says what "git is ready" means: - a minimum git version; - the capabilities other osat managers rely on; - required configuration, such as line endings, `safe.directory`, credential helper, and long paths on Windows. Other managers ask osat-manager-git whether the contract is met, rather than probing git themselves. How git gets installed matters less than whether the contract holds. ## Step three: set the scope The first plan was a thin check-only stub. That changed: the full manager is needed in the short term, because other osat managers need git soon. The agreed scope is: - manage multiple git installations per machine, not just one; - run on Linux, macOS and Windows; - follow the standard osat CLI defined by the osat-manager specification; - provide translated messages, starting with en-ca and fr-ca. Where the osat-manager specification defines commands, output or translation format, the specification takes precedence over this project's own documents. ## Step four: write Universal Cake requirements through a worked example General metrics become useful only when a real task forces them into testable statements. The chosen task is "Add a document" to SAT content, done end to end: 1. The interface asks osat-manager-git whether the baseline is met, and explains any problem in plain language. 2. The person fills in title, description and language. 3. The tool writes a markdown file with Dublin Core front matter and a `urn:uuid:` identifier. 4. The tool records the change in git with a generated message. 5. The person sees "Saved" and a readable history, and can undo with "Remove this change". Each requirement gets an ID, one statement, and a test with a clear pass or fail. They fall into five areas. | Area | Prefix | What it secures | | --- | --- | --- | | Inclusive design | ID | WCAG 2.2 level AA (World Wide Web Consortium [W3C], 2023), keyboard and screen-reader use, plain language, no git terms. | | Multilingual | ML | All strings from a message catalog; en-ca and fr-ca language tags (Phillips & Davis, 2009); git's own output never shown directly. | | Security | SEC | No shell, `--end-of-options` before user input (Git Project, n.d.), safe file names, localhost only, hooks off by default (OWASP Foundation, n.d.). | | Agency and longevity | AL | Plain markdown in standard git, full history, undo, export, no network dependency. | | osat-manager-git | GIT | Discovery, install and removal, active installation per scope, baseline checks, osat CLI conformance, translations, idempotence, signed sources. | These requirements are recorded in the companion document, *Universal Cake Requirements: Add Document Slice*. ## Design principles carried forward These principles came out of the feasibility work and guide later projects, including the web interface. - **The git CLI is the engine.** Parsing git's machine-readable porcelain output gives access to all of git. Libraries such as libgit2 or isomorphic-git are used only where they clearly help, because they do not cover all of git. - **Progressive disclosure.** Common tasks get excellent guided flows; advanced operations stay reachable but out of the way. - **Security from day one.** A service that runs git is attack surface: each repository is sandboxed, and hooks from untrusted repositories are treated as code execution. - **Translate meaning, not git.** Structured results map to the project's own message catalog, so every language gets the same clarity. - **Hardest accessibility first.** Diffs and merge conflicts are the hardest things to make screen-reader friendly, so they are prototyped early. ## Proposed build sequence This order is proposed, not yet confirmed. 1. Write the baseline contract as one versioned file. 2. Build discovery: list every git installation with version, path and origin. 3. Build check: report each installation against the baseline as JSON, following the osat CLI. 4. Build install, upgrade and remove through each platform's native route: apt, dnf, Homebrew and winget. 5. Build active-installation switching per machine and per user. 6. Complete the en-ca and fr-ca catalogs, and test on Linux Mint, Fedora, macOS and Windows 11. 7. Build the Add Document slice on top, and test it against the Universal Cake requirements. ## Before building an interface: evaluate prior art GitHub Desktop, GitButler and Forgejo should be evaluated against the Universal Cake metrics first. The results show which gaps in accessibility, language support and safety a new interface would actually fill. ## Open questions - Which shared commands, output schema and exit codes does the osat-manager specification define? - Which minimum git version does the baseline set? - Can the active installation also be set per SAT node, through the config cascade? - Which Dublin Core and `sat:` fields does the Add Document form collect? - Which languages follow en-ca and fr-ca? - Which license applies to this document? ## Changelog | Date | Version | Change | | --- | --- | --- | | 2026-09-30 | 0.1.0 (provisional) | First draft of the process overview. | ## References Git Project. (n.d.). *gitcli: Git command-line interface and conventions*. Git documentation. https://git-scm.com/docs/gitcli [Return to text](#cite-git-nd-1) OWASP Foundation. (n.d.). *OS command injection defense cheat sheet*. OWASP Cheat Sheet Series. https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/OS_Command_Injection_Defense_Cheat_Sheet.html [Return to text](#cite-owasp-nd-1) Phillips, A., & Davis, M. (2009). *Tags for identifying languages* (BCP 47, RFC 5646). Internet Engineering Task Force. https://doi.org/10.17487/RFC5646 [Return to text](#cite-phillips-2009-1) Steel, C. (n.d.). *Universal Cake evaluation metrics* [Unpublished manuscript, uc-radar repository]. GitHub. https://github.com/steelcj/uc-radar [Return to text](#cite-steel-nd-1) World Wide Web Consortium. (2023). *Web content accessibility guidelines (WCAG) 2.2* (W3C Recommendation). https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/ [Return to text](#cite-w3c-2023-1) --- title: "Universal Cake Requirements: Add Document Slice" description: "Testable Universal Cake requirements for osat-manager-git and a git-backed Add Document interface for SAT content." identifier: "urn:uuid:82642c55-a2c5-4800-9f24-600400f9e195" language: "en-ca" creator: "Christopher Steel" date: "2026-09-30" version: "0.1.0" status: "provisional" relation: "https://github.com/steelcj/uc-radar" --- # Universal Cake Requirements: Add Document Slice This is a provisional draft. The version stays provisional until Christopher Steel confirms it. It was drafted with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic). ## Purpose and scope This document turns the Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics (Steel, n.d.) into testable requirements, using one real task as the worked example: adding a document to SAT content through a friendly, git-backed interface. Every later project, including a full SAT content interface, inherits these requirements rather than starting from zero. Two components are in scope: - **osat-manager-git**, in full: it manages multiple git installations per machine on Linux, macOS and Windows, through the standard osat CLI with translated messages. Other osat managers depend on it. - **The Add Document slice**: a small local web interface that writes one document into SAT content and records it in git, without the person needing to know git. The config cascade resolver is not in scope. The slice uses one fixed content location until the cascade specification is settled. ## The worked example: Add a document

# osat-manager-restic

`manage-restic` installs [restic](https://restic.net/), the encrypted, deduplicating backup program, into your own account. It keeps several versions side by side, switches between them, protects what it installs, and keeps every verified download so a version can be restored without a network. It is the pilot OSAT manager, succeeding osat-fluent-restic-tool.

## Requirements

Python 3.8 or later. The manager uses the standard library only.

## Install

```sh
PYTHONPATH=lib python3 -m osat_manager_restic --self-install
manage-restic --install
restic version
```

On Windows, in Command Prompt, the first line is `set PYTHONPATH=lib` followed by `python -m osat_manager_restic --self-install`.

The launchers go to `~/.local/bin`, or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\osat\bin` on Windows, which must be on your `PATH`. [Using manage-restic](en-ca/docs/guides/usage/using-manage-restic-v0.1.0.md) explains every command.

## Verification

Every download is verified before it is unpacked: the signature on restic's `SHA256SUMS` against restic's signing key, pinned by fingerprint in [`manager.yaml`](manager.yaml), then the download's SHA-256 against that signed list. The binary must then report the requested version. The reasons are in [decision 0001](en-ca/docs/decisions/0001--build-manage-restic-v0.1.0.md).

## Platform status

| Platform | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Linux, amd64 | Verified: the full end-to-end scenario passed on 2026-10-09, in an Incus container (Linux Mint 22.3, Python 3.10) restored to a clean snapshot, including the offline restore from the verified archive. [Record](tests/e2e/linux/2026-10-09--linux-scenario-run.md); passed again on 2026-10-11 after the Windows launcher change. [Record](tests/e2e/linux/2026-10-11--linux-scenario-run.md) |
| Linux, arm64 | Not yet verified |
| macOS | Not yet verified: no Apple hardware available |
| Windows, amd64 | Scenario passed, not yet marked verified: the full end-to-end scenario passed on 2026-10-11, over SSH in a Windows 11 virtual machine restored to a clean snapshot (Python 3.15.0 from manage-python), including the offline restore inside a network cut. The cut's IPv6 internet path could not be tested on this network, so its self-test is to be repeated on a network with IPv6 before Windows is marked verified. [Record](tests/e2e/windows/2026-10-11--windows-test-run.md) |

The version stays below 1.0.0 until every platform is verified (uc-automa 0011).

## Develop

```sh
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/unit
```

The unit tests run offline, against fake releases signed with a test key in `tests/unit/data/`; `OSAT_INSTALL_TESTS=1` adds a wheel install test.

The end-to-end drivers and the network cut live in uc-test-platform (uc-automa 0031). They run on the Linux host that holds the Incus instances. Install uc-test-platform from a checkout beside this one, in its own virtual environment; the Windows driver also takes uc-portage and uc-automa from checkouts beside this one:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/steelcj/uc-test-platform ../uc-test-platform
python -m venv ../uc-test-platform/.venv
../uc-test-platform/.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e ../uc-test-platform
. ../uc-test-platform/.venv/bin/activate
uc-test-platform --version
```

`python` is the command manage-python installs. With another Python, use its own command instead, such as `python3`. On Debian and Ubuntu the system Python's `venv` module needs the `python3-venv` package first: `sudo apt install python3-venv`. Until uc-test-platform's first release, after uc-automa 0.2.0, a run record names the uc-test-platform commit it used.

Then, with that environment active:

```sh
uc-test-platform linux --repository . --instance <container> --snapshot <clean-snapshot>
uc-test-platform windows --repository . --instance <vm> --snapshot <clean-snapshot> --ssh <host>
```

They run `tests/e2e_scenario.py`, which stays here, as an ordinary user, with real downloads, in an Incus container on Linux and over SSH in an Incus virtual machine on Windows, and write their records here, under `tests/e2e/<platform>/`. The Windows driver also runs the unit tests of this repository, uc-portage and uc-automa, the network cut's self-test, and an install of uc-portage and uc-automa from wheels with `pip install --no-index` inside a network cut, with PyYAML built as pure Python.

## License

osat-manager-restic follows the REUSE convention: [`REUSE.toml`](REUSE.toml) records which licence covers which paths, and [`LICENSES/`](LICENSES/) holds their texts. Code is licensed under the MIT License, also in [`LICENSE`](LICENSE). Documentation is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Releases are MIT and CC BY 4.0 from 0.1.0, the first public release (uc-automa 0025). restic's release signature, kept as test data, is restic's, under the BSD 2-Clause License.

This document, *osat-manager-restic*, by **Christopher Steel**, with AI assistance from **Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)**, is licensed under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
# Roadmap

Forward plan only; completed items move to [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

## 0.1.1

Findings of the third independent review of the OpenPGP verifier, none a violation of its five properties:

- Detect a download shorter than its `Content-Length` and retry it, rather than reporting it as a checksum mismatch.
- Refuse a `now` that is not a finite number in `verify`, so a caller cannot switch off the time checks.
- Refuse a critical bit on subpackets in the unhashed area, which nothing signs.
- Test that the manager applies the 1 MiB cap to `SHA256SUMS` and its signature, not only that the constant is small.
- Put an overall time limit on each download, as well as the per-read timeout.

## Next release

- Repeat the network cut's self-test on a network with an IPv6 route, then mark Windows verified; the end-to-end scenario passed on Windows on 2026-10-11, on a network where the IPv6 internet path could not be tested.
- Verify end to end on Linux arm64.
- Verify end to end on macOS, on Apple hardware.

## Later

- Move shared manager behaviour into one installed package, if that open question is answered yes, retiring this manager's own copies of the manifest lookup and the YAML reader.
- Offer to add the launcher directory to `PATH` on Windows.
- A deliberate command to prune old archived versions, refusing the active version.
- Reach 1.0.0 when Linux, macOS and Windows are all verified.

# osat-manager-restic

`manage-restic` installs [restic](https://restic.net/), the encrypted, deduplicating backup program, into your own account. It keeps several versions side by side, switches between them, protects what it installs, and keeps every verified download so a version can be restored without a network. It is the pilot OSAT manager, succeeding osat-fluent-restic-tool.

## Requirements

Python 3.8 or later. The manager uses the standard library only.

## Install

```sh
PYTHONPATH=lib python3 -m osat_manager_restic --self-install
manage-restic --install
restic version
```

On Windows, in Command Prompt, the first line is `set PYTHONPATH=lib` followed by `python -m osat_manager_restic --self-install`.

The launchers go to `~/.local/bin`, or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\osat\bin` on Windows, which must be on your `PATH`. [Using manage-restic](en-ca/docs/guides/usage/using-manage-restic-v0.1.0.md) explains every command.

## Verification

Every download is verified before it is unpacked: the signature on restic's `SHA256SUMS` against restic's signing key, pinned by fingerprint in [`manager.yaml`](manager.yaml), then the download's SHA-256 against that signed list. The binary must then report the requested version. The reasons are in [decision 0001](en-ca/docs/decisions/0001--build-manage-restic-v0.1.0.md).

## Platform status

| Platform | Status |
| --- | --- |
| Linux, amd64 | Verified: the full end-to-end scenario passed on 2026-10-09, in an Incus container (Linux Mint 22.3, Python 3.10) restored to a clean snapshot, including the offline restore from the verified archive. [Record](tests/e2e/linux/2026-10-09--linux-scenario-run.md); passed again on 2026-10-11 after the Windows launcher change. [Record](tests/e2e/linux/2026-10-11--linux-scenario-run.md) |
| Linux, arm64 | Not yet verified |
| macOS | Not yet verified: no Apple hardware available |
| Windows, amd64 | Scenario passed, not yet marked verified: the full end-to-end scenario passed on 2026-10-11, over SSH in a Windows 11 virtual machine restored to a clean snapshot (Python 3.15.0 from manage-python), including the offline restore inside a network cut. The cut's IPv6 internet path could not be tested on this network, so its self-test is to be repeated on a network with IPv6 before Windows is marked verified. [Record](tests/e2e/windows/2026-10-11--windows-test-run.md) |

The version stays below 1.0.0 until every platform is verified (uc-automa 0011).

## Develop

```sh
python3 -m unittest discover -s tests/unit
```

The unit tests run offline, against fake releases signed with a test key in `tests/unit/data/`; `OSAT_INSTALL_TESTS=1` adds a wheel install test.

The end-to-end drivers and the network cut live in uc-test-platform (uc-automa 0031). They run on the Linux host that holds the Incus instances. Install uc-test-platform from a checkout beside this one, in its own virtual environment; the Windows driver also takes uc-portage and uc-automa from checkouts beside this one:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/steelcj/uc-test-platform ../uc-test-platform
python -m venv ../uc-test-platform/.venv
../uc-test-platform/.venv/bin/python -m pip install -e ../uc-test-platform
. ../uc-test-platform/.venv/bin/activate
uc-test-platform --version
```

`python` is the command manage-python installs. With another Python, use its own command instead, such as `python3`. On Debian and Ubuntu the system Python's `venv` module needs the `python3-venv` package first: `sudo apt install python3-venv`. Until uc-test-platform's first release, after uc-automa 0.2.0, a run record names the uc-test-platform commit it used.

Then, with that environment active:

```sh
uc-test-platform linux --repository . --instance <container> --snapshot <clean-snapshot>
uc-test-platform windows --repository . --instance <vm> --snapshot <clean-snapshot> --ssh <host>
```

They run `tests/e2e_scenario.py`, which stays here, as an ordinary user, with real downloads, in an Incus container on Linux and over SSH in an Incus virtual machine on Windows, and write their records here, under `tests/e2e/<platform>/`. The Windows driver also runs the unit tests of this repository, uc-portage and uc-automa, the network cut's self-test, and an install of uc-portage and uc-automa from wheels with `pip install --no-index` inside a network cut, with PyYAML built as pure Python.

## License

osat-manager-restic follows the REUSE convention: [`REUSE.toml`](REUSE.toml) records which licence covers which paths, and [`LICENSES/`](LICENSES/) holds their texts. Code is licensed under the MIT License, also in [`LICENSE`](LICENSE). Documentation is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. Releases are MIT and CC BY 4.0 from 0.1.0, the first public release (uc-automa 0025). restic's release signature, kept as test data, is restic's, under the BSD 2-Clause License.

This document, *osat-manager-restic*, by **Christopher Steel**, with AI assistance from **Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)**, is licensed under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).
# Roadmap

Forward plan only; completed items move to [CHANGELOG.md](CHANGELOG.md).

## 0.1.1

Findings of the third independent review of the OpenPGP verifier, none a violation of its five properties:

- Detect a download shorter than its `Content-Length` and retry it, rather than reporting it as a checksum mismatch.
- Refuse a `now` that is not a finite number in `verify`, so a caller cannot switch off the time checks.
- Refuse a critical bit on subpackets in the unhashed area, which nothing signs.
- Test that the manager applies the 1 MiB cap to `SHA256SUMS` and its signature, not only that the constant is small.
- Put an overall time limit on each download, as well as the per-read timeout.

## Next release

- Repeat the network cut's self-test on a network with an IPv6 route, then mark Windows verified; the end-to-end scenario passed on Windows on 2026-10-11, on a network where the IPv6 internet path could not be tested.
- Verify end to end on Linux arm64.
- Verify end to end on macOS, on Apple hardware.

## Later

- Move shared manager behaviour into one installed package, if that open question is answered yes, retiring this manager's own copies of the manifest lookup and the YAML reader.
- Offer to add the launcher directory to `PATH` on Windows.
- A deliberate command to prune old archived versions, refusing the active version.
- Reach 1.0.0 when Linux, macOS and Windows are all verified.

Only Linux on amd64 is verified for 0.1.0. - **Verification:** every download is checked in two steps before it is unpacked. The signature on `SHA256SUMS` is verified against the key pinned in `manager.yaml`, by fingerprint; then the asset's SHA-256 is compared with the signed list. The extracted binary must then report the requested version before it is placed. - **Signature verification in the standard library:** the process requires the standard library only, with no shell commands, and Windows rarely has `gpg`. The manager therefore verifies the RSA signature itself, implementing the parts of RFC 4880 it needs and refusing the rest. osat-fluent-restic-tool had deferred signature checking for exactly this reason. - **Strict verification rules:** the hash is exactly SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512; the signature's hashed area names the pinned fingerprint as issuer, and an issuer only in the unhashed area, or none, fails; every issuer named must be the pinned key; the 16-bit hash prefix must match; the PKCS#1 v1.5 encoding is compared byte for byte; and malformed or truncated input fails closed. Where these are stricter than `gpg`, the test vectors name the rule. - **Pin the key that actually signs:** the pinned fingerprint names the key that makes the signatures, by its own fingerprint, whether a primary key or a subkey. restic signs with its primary key, `CF8F 18F2 8445 7597 3F79 D4E1 91A6 868B D3F7 A907`. A subkey's binding to its primary is not checked; pinning the subkey's own fingerprint is the trust decision. - **Independent review:** because the verifier is security-critical, new code, it is reviewed independently, by a reviewer who did not see it written, before osat-manager-restic is tagged, and again after any rewrite. This conflicts with the process's own pairing of a YAML manifest with standard-library-only code, and is recorded as a finding about the process. - **Finding manager.yaml:** the manager follows uc-automa 0019, mapping `manager.yaml` into the package and falling back to a proven checkout, but with its own small lookup rather than uc-portage's resolver, since uc-portage is not standard-library-only. This is a second copy of that rule, to be retired if the shared manager package becomes real. - **The verified archive** keeps the downloaded asset with the `SHA256SUMS` and signature that verified it, so an offline restore re-checks both. - **Install and activate together:** `--install` makes the installed version active, because osat-fluent-restic-tool's install that did not activate was misleading. - **Locations:** the install root is `osat/restic` in each platform's per-user data directory, as the process proposes, while whether `osat` is the right name remains open. Launchers go to `~/.local/bin` on Linux and macOS and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\osat\bin` on Windows, which the user adds to `PATH`. - **Nothing left behind:** the manager records each directory it creates outside its install root and removes it on uninstall if it is empty. ## Consequences - The pinned key changes only by a new version of `manager.yaml`, reviewed like any other change. - The manager never touches restic's own configuration, cache, repositories or passwords, and does not use `restic self-update`. - Reaching 1.0.0 needs macOS and Windows verified (uc-automa 0011). ## References restic authors. The signature on `SHA256SUMS` is verified against the key pinned in `manager.yaml`, by fingerprint; then the asset's SHA-256 is compared with the signed list. The extracted binary must then report the requested version before it is placed. - **Signature verification in the standard library:** the process requires the standard library only, with no shell commands, and Windows rarely has `gpg`. The manager therefore verifies the RSA signature itself, implementing the parts of RFC 4880 it needs and refusing the rest. osat-fluent-restic-tool had deferred signature checking for exactly this reason. - **Strict verification rules:** the hash is exactly SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512; the signature's hashed area names the pinned fingerprint as issuer, and an issuer only in the unhashed area, or none, fails; every issuer named must be the pinned key; the 16-bit hash prefix must match; the PKCS#1 v1.5 encoding is compared byte for byte; and malformed or truncated input fails closed. Where these are stricter than `gpg`, the test vectors name the rule. - **Pin the key that actually signs:** the pinned fingerprint names the key that makes the signatures, by its own fingerprint, whether a primary key or a subkey. restic signs with its primary key, `CF8F 18F2 8445 7597 3F79 D4E1 91A6 868B D3F7 A907`. A subkey's binding to its primary is not checked; pinning the subkey's own fingerprint is the trust decision. - **Independent review:** because the verifier is security-critical, new code, it is reviewed independently, by a reviewer who did not see it written, before osat-manager-restic is tagged, and again after any rewrite. Every test vector's expected verdict is confirmed with `gpg --verify`. - **Reading manager.yaml without PyYAML:** the manager must run on the Python manage-python installs, which has no PyYAML, so it reads the strict subset of YAML that `manager.yaml` uses and refuses anything else. This conflicts with the process's own pairing of a YAML manifest with standard-library-only code, and is recorded as a finding about the process. - **Finding manager.yaml:** the manager follows uc-automa 0019, mapping `manager.yaml` into the package and falling back to a proven checkout, but with its own small lookup rather than uc-portage's resolver, since uc-portage is not standard-library-only. This is a second copy of that rule, to be retired if the shared manager package becomes real. - **The verified archive** keeps the downloaded asset with the `SHA256SUMS` and signature that verified it, so an offline restore re-checks both. - **Install and activate together:** `--install` makes the installed version active, because osat-fluent-restic-tool's install that did not activate was misleading. - **Locations:** the install root is `osat/restic` in each platform's per-user data directory, as the process proposes, while whether `osat` is the right name remains open. Launchers go to `~/.local/bin` on Linux and macOS and `%LOCALAPPDATA%\osat\bin` on Windows, which the user adds to `PATH`. - **Nothing left behind:** the manager records each directory it creates outside its install root and removes it on uninstall if it is empty. ## Consequences - The pinned key changes only by a new version of `manager.yaml`, reviewed like any other change. - The manager never touches restic's own configuration, cache, repositories or passwords, and does not use `restic self-update`. - Reaching 1.0.0 needs macOS and Windows verified (uc-automa 0011). ## References restic authors. (n.d.). *Installation*. restic documentation. Retrieved October 9, 2026, from https://restic.readthedocs.io/en/stable/020_installation.html [↩](#cite-restic-nd) Steel, C. (2026a). *Creating an OSAT manager repository* (Version 0.2.0) [Unpublished manuscript]. uc-automa. urn:uuid:b18e2ed3-b364-4880-b3c7-5676961f0174 [↩](#cite-steel-2026a) ## Changelog | Version | Date | Status | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0.1.0 | 2026-10-09 | Accepted | Initial version | ## License This document, *Decision: Build manage-restic*, by **Christopher Steel**, with AI assistance from **Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)**, is licensed under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

content.content: --- title: "Creating an OSAT Manager Repository" dc:title: "Creating an OSAT Manager Repository" dc:creator: "Christopher Steel" dc:contributor: "Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic), AI assistance" dc:subject: "OSAT managers, repository creation, uc-automa, offerings, cross-platform testing, release" dc:description: "The process for creating a new osat-manager repository with uc-automa, from radar assessment to first release, in ten stages with gates." dc:date: "2026-10-11" dc:type: "Text" dc:format: "text/markdown" dc:identifier: "urn:uuid:b18e2ed3-b364-4880-b3c7-5676961f0174" dc:source: "Hand-off package 2026-10-09--uc-automa-foundation, inputs/revise/osat-manager--creating-a-new-repository-v0.1.0.md, not under version control" dc:language: "en-CA" dc:rights: "CC-BY-4.0" sat:version: "0.4.0" sat:status: "Accepted" --- # Creating an OSAT Manager Repository Version: 0.4.0 Status: Accepted ## Summary A new OSAT manager goes through ten stages, from a radar assessment of the tool it manages to its first release, and each stage ends at a checkable gate. The repository is created fresh, receives everything shared by subscribing to uc-automa's offerings, and copies nothing by hand. Its layout type is `osat-manager`, described in the directory guide [(Steel, 2026a)](#ref-steel-2026a). ## What an OSAT manager is An OSAT manager is a governed tool that installs another tool into user space and manages its versions there, with no elevated privilege, no system package manager and no compiler. The contract below is drawn from osat-manager-python, the first manager, which installs self-contained CPython runtimes and runs as `manage-python` [(Steel, 2026c)](#ref-steel-2026c). Every manager meets the same contract, so a person who has used one can use them all. | Capability | What it means | | --- | --- | | User-space install | Installs into the user's own directories; never needs administrator rights | | Versions side by side | Several versions of the managed tool can be installed at once | | Switching | One command makes a chosen version the active one | | Aliases | A generic alias, such as `restic`, beside versioned ones, such as `restic-0.18`; any alias can be renamed | | Protection | Installed versions are guarded against accidental modification | | Nothing left behind | Uninstalling removes everything the manager owns, and a parent directory such as `~/.local/bin` only if the manager created it and it is now empty; a directory that holds anything else is never removed | | Verified archive | Every download is verified before it is unpacked, and kept with the checksums and signature that verified it, so a version can be restored offline and re-checked | | Self-install | The manager installs itself, so it works from any directory | | Three platforms | Linux, macOS and Windows, with each platform's status stated honestly | ## Naming | Thing | Pattern | Example | | --- | --- | --- | | Repository | `osat-manager-` | `osat-manager-restic` | | Command | `manage-` | `manage-restic` | | Python package | `osat_manager_` | `osat_manager_restic` | | SAT sidecar | `.osat-manager-.assets/` | `.osat-manager-restic.assets/` | | Documents before 1.0.0 | `-vX.Y.Z.md` | `using-manage-restic-v0.1.0.md` | | Documents from 1.0.0 | `.md` | `using-manage-restic.md` | `` is the managed tool's own name in lowercase, with hyphens for any spaces. The Python package uses underscores, because Python cannot import hyphens; everything else uses hyphens. ## Repository layout The `osat-manager` layout extends `python-tool`, which extends `base`. `uc-automa check` compares the repository with it. ```text osat-manager-/ ├── README.md what it manages, install, platform status table ├── LICENSE from license-mit ├── LICENSES/ from the licence offerings ├── REUSE.toml seeded by reuse ├── CHANGELOG.md seeded by changelog ├── VERSION seeded by version-file ├── ROADMAP.md ├── CONTRIBUTING.md ├── CLAUDE.md ends with the claude-signpost block ├── .uc-automa.yaml written once by uc-automa init ├── .uc-portage-state.yaml written by uc-automa offerings apply ├── .osat-manager-.assets/ │ ├── archive.yaml │ └── dc.yaml ├── .gitattributes from line-endings ├── .editorconfig from editorconfig ├── .gitignore ├── pyproject.toml the package and the manage- entry point ├── manager.yaml what is managed, from where, how it is verified ├── lib/ │ └── osat_manager_/ ├── tests/ │ ├── unit/ offline, run everywhere │ └── e2e/ │ └── linux/ one directory per platform run └── en-ca/ └── docs/ ├── README.md generated by uc-automa docs index ├── guides/ using the manager └── decisions/ decisions for this manager only ``` ## The process at a glance ```mermaid flowchart TD s1["Assess the tool on the radar"] s2["Record the decision"] s3["Create the repository"] s4["Subscribe to uc-automa"] s5["Describe the managed tool"] s6["Implement the manager"] s7["Test on each platform"] s8["Document"] s9["Release"] s10["Register and retire"] s1 --> s2 --> s3 --> s4 --> s5 --> s6 --> s7 --> s8 --> s9 --> s10 s7 -- "a platform fails" --> s6 ``` ## Assess the tool on the radar Every manager starts with the tool it manages, so the tool is evaluated before any code is written. Write a uc-radar entry using the radar's entry template and the Universal Cake evaluation metrics [(Steel, 2026d)](#ref-steel-2026d). Adding the entry to uc-radar goes through its own review; until then it is a draft. The entry answers the questions a manager depends on: - Does upstream publish prebuilt releases for Linux, macOS and Windows, and for which architectures? - Does upstream publish checksums, and are they signed? With what key? - Can the tool run from a user directory without installation or administrator rights? - What licence does the tool carry, and does it allow keeping a verified archive? - How often does upstream release, and how are versions named? Gate: the tool is in the `trial` or `adopt` ring, or the entry explains why a manager is still wanted. ## Record the decision Draft the decision to build the manager before the repository exists, outside any repository, such as in the hand-off folder for the work. It becomes `en-ca/docs/decisions/0001---v0.1.0.md`, numbered within the repository, in the repository's first commit. It names the managed tool, the radar entry, the platforms targeted first, and anything this manager does differently from the contract. Gate: the decision record is drafted. ## Create the repository Create the repository fresh and empty, with no forge-generated files, so its first commit already conforms. 1. Create the local repository with `git init`. Creating it on a forge and pushing are Christopher Steel's decisions, taken separately. 2. Generate the repository's identifier with `uuidgen -r`. 3. Write `.osat-manager-.assets/archive.yaml` and `dc.yaml`. 4. Place the drafted decision record at `en-ca/docs/decisions/0001---v0.1.0.md`, and commit it with the sidecar as the repository's first commit. ```yaml # .osat-manager-.assets/archive.yaml sat:role: "archive" dc:identifier: "urn:uuid:" dc:title: "osat-manager-" dc:language: "en-CA" dc:rights: "CC-BY-4.0" ``` Gate: the first commit holds the sidecar and the decision record, and nothing else. ## Subscribe to uc-automa Everything shared arrives from uc-automa by subscription; nothing is copied by hand. Install uc-automa from its release tag into the environment you work in, together with uc-portage, which it depends on. uc-portage is not on a package index, so both are named in the same command; installing uc-automa alone fails to find it. ```sh python3 -m pip install "git+https://github.com/steelcj/uc-portage@v0.1.0" \ "git+https://github.com/steelcj/uc-automa@v0.1.0" uc-automa --version ``` The installed version is the one `init` pins, and every later `uc-automa` command requires the pin and the installed version to match (uc-automa 0020). `init` writes `.uc-automa.yaml` once, with the subscriptions the osat-manager layout requires (uc-automa 0023); the repository owns the file from then on. ```sh uc-automa init --repository osat-manager- --layout osat-manager uc-automa offerings plan uc-automa offerings apply git add -A git commit -m "Receive uc-automa offerings" ``` A repository that file-fairy served before, such as an existing manager moving to this process, still holds the blocks file-fairy managed, marked `` and ``, usually `claude-md-signpost` in `CLAUDE.md`. uc-portage takes over only blocks marked `` with a name its offerings deliver, and uc-automa delivers its signpost as `uc-automa-signpost`, so an old block is never taken over, and renaming its markers does not help. Delete each old `fairy:` block, markers and contents, by hand, in the same commit as the first apply; otherwise its stale text stays beside the new block. A licence that file-fairy delivered as a block now arrives as `LICENSE` and `LICENSES/` files instead. Gate: `uc-automa offerings plan` reports nothing to do, and no `fairy:begin` marker is left in the repository. ## Describe the managed tool Write `manager.yaml`, a declarative description of what the manager installs, where it comes from, how each download is verified, and what each platform needs. Keeping this in data rather than code means most managers differ only in this file, and a reviewer can check sources and verification without reading code. ```yaml # manager.yaml (illustrative; every value comes from the radar entry) tool: name: "" command: "manage-" upstream: "" license: "" versions: scheme: "semver" default_alias: "" versioned_alias: "-{major}.{minor}" sources: release_url: "" checksums_url: "" signature_url: "" verification: checksum: "sha256" signature: "" keep_verified_archive: true platforms: linux: {arch: ["x86_64", "aarch64"], status: "planned"} macos: {arch: ["x86_64", "arm64"], status: "planned"} windows: {arch: ["x86_64"], status: "planned"} ``` If upstream signs its checksums, pin its signing key by fingerprint, and confirm the fingerprint from two independent sources, such as upstream's documentation and the key server it names. Gate: every source and verification field is filled from the radar entry, with no placeholders left. ## Implement the manager Implement the contract in `lib/osat_manager_/`, reading `manager.yaml` for everything tool-specific, and expose it as a console-script entry point, which gives a native launcher on Windows and a script on Linux and macOS from one definition [(Python Packaging Authority, n.d.)](#ref-pypa-nd). - Standard library and `pathlib`, with no shell commands at runtime, so behaviour is the same on every platform. Tests may call other tools, such as `gpg`, to cross-check results. - Shared behaviour comes from the shared manager package (uc-automa 0024): reading `manager.yaml` without PyYAML, finding it in an install or a checkout, and verifying OpenPGP signatures. Until that package exists, a manager carries its own copies, listed as known debt. - A signature verifier is reviewed independently, by a reviewer who did not see it written, before any manager relying on it is tagged. - Platform differences, such as install locations and alias launchers, are resolved in one module. - Every download is verified with SHA-256 before it is unpacked, and against upstream's signature if upstream signs its checksums. The verified archive is kept. - `manager.yaml` is read from the repository root through the shared data resolver, so the installed package carries it (uc-automa 0019). Gate: `tests/unit/` passes offline. ## Test on each platform Each platform has its own end-to-end run, and each run updates the platform status table. A platform is either verified end to end or stated as not yet verified; it is never assumed (uc-automa 0011). | Platform | Where it runs | Record | | --- | --- | --- | | Linux | An Incus container restored to a clean snapshot before and after the run, as an ordinary user | `tests/e2e/linux/` | | Windows | The Windows 11 virtual machine, reached through its built-in OpenSSH Server with key authentication, as an ordinary user, restored to a snapshot before each run | `tests/e2e/windows/` | | macOS | Apple hardware, the only legitimate place to run macOS | `tests/e2e/macos/` | ```yaml # The end-to-end scenario every platform runs scenario: - "Install the manager into a clean user account" - "Install two versions of the managed tool side by side" - "Switch between them and confirm the active version" - "Rename an alias and confirm both forms resolve correctly" - "Attempt to modify an installed version and confirm it is protected" - "Remove a version, disconnect the network, and restore it from the verified archive" - "Uninstall the manager and confirm nothing is left behind" ``` A scenario run writes a record of every step beside its driver. Upstream files kept as test data, such as `SHA256SUMS`, keep their upstream names inside a zip file, because those names do not follow the naming directives. Gate: every platform in `manager.yaml` is `verified` or has a stated reason it is not. ## Document Write what a user needs, and nothing uc-automa already says. - `README.md`: what the manager manages, how to install it, and the platform status table from testing. - `en-ca/docs/guides/usage/using-manage--v0.1.0.md`: every command, with examples. - `ROADMAP.md`: what is planned, such as unverified platforms. - `CHANGELOG.md`: the entry for the first release, under `[Unreleased]`. - `uc-automa docs index`, to regenerate the documentation index. Gate: `uc-automa check` passes. ## Release The first release is 0.1.0. Until uc-automa provides the release ceremony, planned for uc-automa 0.2.0, a release is tagged by hand, and only with Christopher Steel's approval: a surgical commit that only rolls `CHANGELOG.md` to `## [0.1.0] - `, then an annotated tag `v0.1.0` whose message names the repository and the version, as the directive `release/annotated-version-tags` requires. A manager reaches 1.0.0 when every platform in `manager.yaml` is verified and the full scenario passes on each (uc-automa 0011); its documents then drop the version from their filenames (uc-automa 0002). Gate: the tag exists, approved. ## Register and retire Make the new manager findable, and retire what it replaces. 1. Update the tool's radar entry to link to the manager. 2. Add the manager to the list of OSAT managers, wherever that list is kept (see open questions). 3. If the manager replaces an older `osat-fluent--tool` repository, Christopher Steel adds a README notice naming the successor and archives the old repository, once the new repository is pushed, so the notice links to a real successor. It is not deleted or renamed, so every existing link and clone still works. Gate: a person starting from the radar entry, the OSAT list or the old repository arrives at the new manager. ## Checklist - [ ] Radar entry written for the tool, ring `trial` or `adopt` - [ ] Decision record drafted outside the repository - [ ] Repository created, first commit holding the sidecar and the decision record - [ ] uc-automa installed from its release tag, `uc-automa init` run, offerings applied and committed, old `fairy:` blocks removed - [ ] `manager.yaml` complete, with no placeholders - [ ] Manager implemented; unit tests pass offline - [ ] Linux, Windows and macOS each verified or stated as not yet verified - [ ] README, guide, roadmap and changelog written; `uc-automa check` passes - [ ] 0.1.0 tagged, with approval - [ ] Radar entry linked, manager listed, any predecessor archived with a notice ## Open questions - [ ] Where is the list of OSAT managers kept: in uc-automa, in uc-radar, or in its own repository? - [ ] Is `osat` the right directory name inside each platform's per-user data location? ## References Python Packaging Authority. (n.d.). *Entry points specification*. Python Packaging User Guide. Retrieved October 7, 2026, from https://packaging.python.org/en/latest/specifications/entry-points/ [↩](#cite-pypa-nd) Steel, C. (2026a). *Directory guide* (Version 0.2.0) [Unpublished manuscript]. uc-automa. [directory-guide-v0.2.0.md](../repository/directory-guide-v0.2.0.md) [↩](#cite-steel-2026a) Steel, C. (2026c). *osat-manager-python* [Computer software]. GitHub. https://github.com/steelcj/osat-manager-python [↩](#cite-steel-2026c) Steel, C. (2026d). *uc-radar: Universal Cake radar entries and evaluation metrics* [Computer software]. GitHub. https://github.com/steelcj/uc-radar [↩](#cite-steel-2026d) ## Changelog | Version | Date | Status | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0.4.0 | 2026-10-11 | Accepted | Subscribe stage: installing uc-automa and uc-portage from their release tags, and removing blocks file-fairy managed, which uc-portage never takes over | | 0.3.0 | 2026-10-09 | Accepted | Findings from building osat-manager-restic: the decision drafted before the repository and placed in its first commit, nothing left behind, the shared manager package, pinned keys confirmed twice, independent review of a verifier, snapshot-based Linux runs and the Windows route, upstream names inside zips, the release tag rule, archiving after push | | 0.2.0 | 2026-10-09 | Accepted | Revised to the foundation brief: uc-automa init and offerings instead of .automa.yaml and the interim file-fairy route, en-ca, the osat-manager layout, the three licences, by-hand tagging until the release ceremony, D11 settled; relicensed CC-BY-SA-4.0 | | 0.1.0 | 2026-10-09 | Draft | Initial process: manager contract, naming, layout, ten stages with gates, interim route, checklist | ## License This document, *Creating an OSAT Manager Repository*, by **Christopher Steel**, with AI assistance from **Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)**, is licensed under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

The Python package uses underscores, because Python cannot import hyphens; everything else uses hyphens. ## Repository layout The `osat-manager` layout extends `python-tool`, which extends `base`. `uc-automa check` compares the repository with it. ```text osat-manager-/ ├── README.md what it manages, install, platform status table ├── LICENSE from license-mit ├── LICENSES/ from the licence offerings ├── REUSE.toml seeded by reuse ├── CHANGELOG.md seeded by changelog ├── VERSION seeded by version-file ├── ROADMAP.md ├── CONTRIBUTING.md ├── CLAUDE.md ends with the claude-signpost block ├── .uc-automa.yaml written once by uc-automa init ├── .uc-portage-state.yaml written by uc-automa offerings apply ├── .osat-manager-.assets/ │ ├── archive.yaml │ └── dc.yaml ├── .gitattributes from line-endings ├── .editorconfig from editorconfig ├── .gitignore ├── pyproject.toml the package and the manage- entry point ├── manager.yaml what is managed, from where, how it is verified ├── lib/ │ └── osat_manager_/ ├── tests/ │ ├── unit/ offline, run everywhere │ └── e2e/ │ └── linux/ one directory per platform run └── en-ca/ └── docs/ ├── README.md generated by uc-automa docs index ├── guides/ using the manager └── decisions/ decisions for this manager only ``` ## The process at a glance ```mermaid flowchart TD s1["Assess the tool on the radar"] s2["Record the decision"] s3["Create the repository"] s4["Subscribe to uc-automa"] s5["Describe the managed tool"] s6["Implement the manager"] s7["Test on each platform"] s8["Document"] s9["Release"] s10["Register and retire"] s1 --> s2 --> s3 --> s4 --> s5 --> s6 --> s7 --> s8 --> s9 --> s10 s7 -- "a platform fails" --> s6 ``` ## Assess the tool on the radar Every manager starts with the tool it manages, so the tool is evaluated before any code is written. Write a uc-radar entry using the radar's entry template and the Universal Cake evaluation metrics [(Steel, 2026d)](#ref-steel-2026d). Adding the entry to uc-radar goes through its own review; until then it is a draft. The entry answers the questions a manager depends on: - Does upstream publish prebuilt releases for Linux, macOS and Windows, and for which architectures? - Does upstream publish checksums, and are they signed? With what key? - Can the tool run from a user directory without installation or administrator rights? - What licence does the tool carry, and does it allow keeping a verified archive? - How often does upstream release, and how are versions named? Gate: the tool is in the `trial` or `adopt` ring, or the entry explains why a manager is still wanted. ## Record the decision Draft the decision to build the manager before the repository exists, outside any repository, such as in the hand-off folder for the work. It becomes `en-ca/docs/decisions/0001---v0.1.0.md`, numbered within the repository, in the repository's first commit. It names the managed tool, the radar entry, the platforms targeted first, and anything this manager does differently from the contract. Gate: the decision record is drafted. ## Create the repository Create the repository fresh and empty, with no forge-generated files, so its first commit already conforms. 1. Create the local repository with `git init`. Creating it on a forge and pushing are Christopher Steel's decisions, taken separately. 2. Generate the repository's identifier with `uuidgen -r`. 3. Write `.osat-manager-.assets/archive.yaml` and `dc.yaml`. 4. Place the drafted decision record at `en-ca/docs/decisions/0001---v0.1.0.md`, and commit it with the sidecar as the repository's first commit. ```yaml # .osat-manager-.assets/archive.yaml sat:role: "archive" dc:identifier: "urn:uuid:" dc:title: "osat-manager-" dc:language: "en-CA" dc:rights: "CC-BY-4.0" ``` Gate: the first commit holds the sidecar and the decision record, and nothing else. ## Subscribe to uc-automa Everything shared arrives from uc-automa by subscription; nothing is copied by hand. Install uc-automa from its release tag into the environment you work in, together with uc-portage, which it depends on. uc-portage is not on a package index, so both are named in the same command; installing uc-automa alone fails to find it. ```sh python3 -m pip install "git+https://github.com/steelcj/uc-portage@v0.1.0" \ "git+https://github.com/steelcj/uc-automa@v0.1.0" uc-automa --version ``` The installed version is the one `init` pins, and every later `uc-automa` command requires the pin and the installed version to match (uc-automa 0020). `init` writes `.uc-automa.yaml` once, with the subscriptions the osat-manager layout requires (uc-automa 0023); the repository owns the file from then on. ```sh uc-automa init --repository osat-manager- --layout osat-manager uc-automa offerings plan uc-automa offerings apply git add -A git commit -m "Receive uc-automa offerings" ``` A repository that file-fairy served before, such as an existing manager moving to this process, still holds the blocks file-fairy managed, marked `` and ``, usually `claude-md-signpost` in `CLAUDE.md`. uc-portage takes over only blocks marked `` with a name its offerings deliver, and uc-automa delivers its signpost as `uc-automa-signpost`, so an old block is never taken over, and renaming its markers does not help. Delete each old `fairy:` block, markers and contents, by hand, in the same commit as the first apply; otherwise its stale text stays beside the new block. A licence that file-fairy delivered as a block now arrives as `LICENSE` and `LICENSES/` files instead. Gate: `uc-automa offerings plan` reports nothing to do, and no `fairy:begin` marker is left in the repository. ## Describe the managed tool Write `manager.yaml`, a declarative description of what the manager installs, where it comes from, how each download is verified, and what each platform needs. Keeping this in data rather than code means most managers differ only in this file, and a reviewer can check sources and verification without reading code. ```yaml # manager.yaml (illustrative; every value comes from the radar entry) tool: name: "" command: "manage-" upstream: "" license: "" versions: scheme: "semver" default_alias: "" versioned_alias: "-{major}.{minor}" sources: release_url: "" checksums_url: "" signature_url: "" verification: checksum: "sha256" signature: "" keep_verified_archive: true platforms: linux: {arch: ["x86_64", "aarch64"], status: "planned"} macos: {arch: ["x86_64", "arm64"], status: "planned"} windows: {arch: ["x86_64"], status: "planned"} ``` If upstream signs its checksums, pin its signing key by fingerprint, and confirm the fingerprint from two independent sources, such as upstream's documentation and the key server it names. Gate: every source and verification field is filled from the radar entry, with no placeholders left. ## Implement the manager Implement the contract in `lib/osat_manager_/`, reading `manager.yaml` for everything tool-specific, and expose it as a console-script entry point, which gives a native launcher on Windows and a script on Linux and macOS from one definition [(Python Packaging Authority, n.d.)](#ref-pypa-nd). - Standard library and `pathlib`, with no shell commands at runtime, so behaviour is the same on every platform. Tests may call other tools, such as `gpg`, to cross-check results. - Shared behaviour comes from the shared manager package (uc-automa 0024): reading `manager.yaml` without PyYAML, finding it in an install or a checkout, and verifying OpenPGP signatures. Until that package exists, a manager carries its own copies, listed as known debt. - A signature verifier is reviewed independently, by a reviewer who did not see it written, before any manager relying on it is tagged. - Platform differences, such as install locations and alias launchers, are resolved in one module. - Every download is verified with SHA-256 before it is unpacked, and against upstream's signature if upstream signs its checksums. The verified archive is kept. - `manager.yaml` is read from the repository root through the shared data resolver, so the installed package carries it (uc-automa 0019). Gate: `tests/unit/` passes offline. ## Test on each platform Each platform has its own end-to-end run, and each run updates the platform status table. A platform is either verified end to end or stated as not yet verified; it is never assumed (uc-automa 0011). | Platform | Where it runs | Record | | --- | --- | --- | | Linux | An Incus container restored to a clean snapshot before and after the run, as an ordinary user | `tests/e2e/linux/` | | Windows | The Windows 11 virtual machine, reached through its built-in OpenSSH Server with key authentication, as an ordinary user, restored to a snapshot before each run | `tests/e2e/windows/` | | macOS | Apple hardware, the only legitimate place to run macOS | `tests/e2e/macos/` | ```yaml # The end-to-end scenario every platform runs scenario: - "Install the manager into a clean user account" - "Install two versions of the managed tool side by side" - "Switch between them and confirm the active version" - "Rename an alias and confirm both forms resolve correctly" - "Attempt to modify an installed version and confirm it is protected" - "Remove a version, disconnect the network, and restore it from the verified archive" - "Uninstall the manager and confirm nothing is left behind" ``` A scenario run writes a record of every step beside its driver. Upstream files kept as test data, such as `SHA256SUMS`, keep their upstream names inside a zip file, because those names do not follow the naming directives. Gate: every platform in `manager.yaml` is `verified` or has a stated reason it is not. ## Document Write what a user needs, and nothing uc-automa already says. - `README.md`: what the manager manages, how to install it, and the platform status table from testing. - `en-ca/docs/guides/usage/using-manage--v0.1.0.md`: every command, with examples. - `ROADMAP.md`: what is planned, such as unverified platforms. - `CHANGELOG.md`: the entry for the first release, under `[Unreleased]`. - `uc-automa docs index`, to regenerate the documentation index. Gate: `uc-automa check` passes. ## Release The first release is 0.1.0. Until uc-automa provides the release ceremony, planned for uc-automa 0.2.0, a release is tagged by hand, and only with Christopher Steel's approval: a surgical commit that only rolls `CHANGELOG.md` to `## [0.1.0] - `, then an annotated tag `v0.1.0` whose message names the repository and the version, as the directive `release/annotated-version-tags` requires. A manager reaches 1.0.0 when every platform in `manager.yaml` is verified and the full scenario passes on each (uc-automa 0011); its documents then drop the version from their filenames (uc-automa 0002). Gate: the tag exists, approved. ## Register and retire Make the new manager findable, and retire what it replaces. 1. Update the tool's radar entry to link to the manager. 2. Add the manager to the list of OSAT managers, wherever that list is kept (see open questions). 3. If the manager replaces an older `osat-fluent--tool` repository, Christopher Steel adds a README notice naming the successor and archives the old repository, once the new repository is pushed, so the notice links to a real successor. It is not deleted or renamed, so every existing link and clone still works. Gate: a person starting from the radar entry, the OSAT list or the old repository arrives at the new manager. ## Checklist - [ ] Radar entry written for the tool, ring `trial` or `adopt` - [ ] Decision record drafted outside the repository - [ ] Repository created, first commit holding the sidecar and the decision record - [ ] uc-automa installed from its release tag, `uc-automa init` run, offerings applied and committed, old `fairy:` blocks removed - [ ] `manager.yaml` complete, with no placeholders - [ ] Manager implemented; unit tests pass offline - [ ] Linux, Windows and macOS each verified or stated as not yet verified - [ ] README, guide, roadmap and changelog written; `uc-automa check` passes - [ ] 0.1.0 tagged, with approval - [ ] Radar entry linked, manager listed, any predecessor archived with a notice ## Open questions - [ ] Where is the list of OSAT managers kept: in uc-automa, in uc-radar, or in its own repository? - [ ] Is `osat` the right directory name inside each platform's per-user data location? ## References Python Packaging Authority. (2026d). *uc-radar: Universal Cake radar entries and evaluation metrics* [Computer software]. GitHub. https://github.com/steelcj/uc-radar [↩](#cite-steel-2026d) ## Changelog | Version | Date | Status | Notes | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 0.4.0 | 2026-10-11 | Accepted | Subscribe stage: installing uc-automa and uc-portage from their release tags, and removing blocks file-fairy managed, which uc-portage never takes over | | 0.3.0 | 2026-10-09 | Accepted | Findings from building osat-manager-restic: the decision drafted before the repository and placed in its first commit, nothing left behind, the shared manager package, pinned keys confirmed twice, independent review of a verifier, snapshot-based Linux runs and the Windows route, upstream names inside zips, the release tag rule, archiving after push | | 0.2.0 | 2026-10-09 | Accepted | Revised to the foundation brief: uc-automa init and offerings instead of .automa.yaml and the interim file-fairy route, en-ca, the osat-manager layout, the three licences, by-hand tagging until the release ceremony, D11 settled; relicensed CC-BY-SA-4.0 | | 0.1.0 | 2026-10-09 | Draft | Initial process: manager contract, naming, layout, ten stages with gates, interim route, checklist | ## License This document, *Creating an OSAT Manager Repository*, by **Christopher Steel**, with AI assistance from **Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)**, is licensed under the [Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/).

---

# UC Radar Entry Template

## Description

A raw markdown template used to create new uc-radar entries. The evaluation body follows the pillars defined in the current [Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics](#universal-cake-evaluation-metrics), so a completed entry and the metrics document use the same vocabulary throughout.

By default new entries go in the `assess` ring unless they document
an item that has been adopted informally and is currently relied upon
in dev, stage, or prod.

The radar uses five states, `assess`, `trial`, `adopt`, `hold`, and
`rejected`. See
[UC Radar Evaluation Lifecycle](#uc-radar--evaluation-lifecycle) for
the full state definitions and transitions.

## Notes

- The leading colon in the heading example below (`:hugo--static-site-generator`)
  is a legacy convention from an earlier naming version. Current slug
  convention per ADR-015 uses double hyphen as a grouping separator
  without a leading colon. This has not been reconciled with the
  no-version, double-hyphen-plus-tagline convention used by existing
  radar entries, see the open item in the radar README.
- `<calculated>` in front matter means the value is derived at
  document creation time — by the author, a tool, or the uc-radar
  preseed mechanism once implemented.
- Every evaluation pass, automated or human, is recorded in the
  `uc-radar_evaluation` block, not in prose alone.
- Rating, evidence tag, and gate conventions below are defined in
  full in the Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics document. This
  template does not restate that guidance, it only provides the
  fields to fill in.

---

## The Radar Entry Template

Copy the contents below and paste into a new markdown document to
create your radar entry.

`````markdown
---
dcterms:title: ""
dcterms:version: "0.1.0"
dcterms:creator: ""
dcterms:contributor: ""
dcterms:subject:
  - "radar"
  - ""
dcterms:description: ""
dcterms:publisher: ""
dcterms:created: ""
dcterms:modified: ""
`````

# UC Radar Entry Template

## Description

A raw markdown template used to create new uc-radar entries. The evaluation body follows the pillars defined in the current [Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics](#universal-cake-evaluation-metrics), so a completed entry and the metrics document use the same vocabulary throughout.

By default new entries go in the `assess` ring unless they document
an item that has been adopted informally and is currently relied upon
in dev, stage, or prod.

The radar uses five states, `assess`, `trial`, `adopt`, `hold`, and
`rejected`. See
[UC Radar Evaluation Lifecycle](#uc-radar--evaluation-lifecycle) for
the full state definitions and transitions.

## Notes

- The leading colon in the heading example below (`:hugo--static-site-generator`)
  is a legacy convention from an earlier naming version. Current slug
  convention per ADR-015 uses double hyphen as a grouping separator
  without a leading colon. This has not been reconciled with the
  no-version, double-hyphen-plus-tagline convention used by existing
  radar entries, see the open item in the radar README.
- `<calculated>` in front matter means the value is derived at
  document creation time — by the author, a tool, or the uc-radar
  preseed mechanism once implemented.
- Every evaluation pass, automated or human, is recorded in the
  `uc-radar_evaluation` block, not in prose alone.
- Rating, evidence tag, and gate conventions below are defined in
  full in the Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics document. This
  template does not restate that guidance, it only provides the
  fields to fill in.
