115:Install both, or just `entire` if you never clone over `entire://`. Git finds the helper by name on `$PATH`, which is what `go install` produces, so nothing else needs configuring. Like git itself, the helper honours `GIT_HTTP_USER_AGENT` for the HTTP `User-Agent` it sends.
128:After the initial setup, use `entire agent` to add or remove agents, `entire configure` to update non-agent settings, and `entire enable` / `entire disable` to toggle Entire on or off.
172:On a repo that has not been enabled yet, `entire enable` runs the initial enable flow: it creates Entire settings, installs git hooks, and prompts you to choose which agent hooks to install. To enable a specific agent non-interactively, use `entire enable --agent <name>` (for example, `entire enable --agent cursor`).
177:- Use `entire agent` to add or remove agents.
178:- Use `entire configure` to update non-agent settings (telemetry, hooks, checkpoint remote, summary provider).
180:The hooks capture session data as you work. Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit. Your code commits stay clean, Entire never creates commits on your active branch. Session metadata is stored outside your branch's history, in the checkpoint storage described under [Checkpoint Storage](#checkpoint-storage).
186:- If a hook manager reinstalls its hooks later, Entire's hooks come back on the next agent turn or `entire enable`, chained to the hook manager's version. If the hook already had a `<hook>.pre-entire` copy, the hook manager's version takes its place and runs after Entire's; the older copy is kept as `<hook>.pre-entire.<timestamp>` and no longer runs, with a warning naming the file.
189:### 2. Work with Your AI Agent
191:Just use one of your AI agents as before. Entire runs in the background, tracking your session:
199:To restore the latest checkpointed session metadata for a branch:
202:entire session resume <branch>
205:Entire checks out the branch, restores the latest checkpointed session metadata (one or more sessions), and prints command(s) to continue.
219:A **session** represents a complete interaction with your AI agent, from start to finish. Each session captures all prompts, responses, files modified, and timestamps.
221:The session ID is the unique identifier the agent itself provides — Entire never mints its own — so an ID you see in `entire session list` is the same one the agent uses. The format is the agent's to choose: most supply a UUID (e.g. `019efea2-b46a-7cbc-be01-4c13460f5019`), while OpenCode uses `ses_`-prefixed IDs.
223:Sessions are stored separately from your code commits, in the repo's checkpoint storage.
225:### Checkpoints
227:A **checkpoint** is a snapshot within a session—a "save point" in your work.
229:Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit, and the commit carries an `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` trailer linking the two.
231:**Checkpoint IDs** are 26-character ULIDs (e.g. `REDACTED`), which sort by creation time. Checkpoints written by older versions of Entire carry a legacy 12-character hex ID (e.g. `a3b2c4d5e6f7`); both formats stay readable in the same repo, and you can pass either to any command that takes a checkpoint ID.
233:### Checkpoint Storage
235:Checkpoints live in your repository's own git object store, never in your branch's history. Each checkpoint is its own git ref:
238:refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>
241:The ref points at a commit whose tree *is* that checkpoint — `metadata.json`, the per-session transcript files, and any subagent task records. `<shard>` is the last two characters of the ID, which keeps the refs evenly distributed.
243:Because checkpoints are independent refs, they are written, pushed, and fetched independently. There is no shared branch tip for concurrent sessions to contend on, and a reader can fetch exactly the one checkpoint it needs instead of a whole history. A checkpoint written on another machine is fetched on demand the first time you read it.
249:  "checkpoints": {
258:git for-each-ref refs/entire/checkpoints    # the raw refs
259:entire checkpoint list                      # checkpoints on this branch
260:entire checkpoint explain <id>              # one checkpoint in full
266:Your Branch                      Checkpoint storage
271:     │  ┌─── Agent works ───┐           │
278:[Your Commit] ─────────────────► [Checkpoint]
279:  Entire-Checkpoint: <id>          (transcript, prompts,
284:As you work, Entire tracks which files the agent touched (and their content hashes) in local session state, alongside a local copy of the transcript; nothing is written to git until you commit. When you commit, that work is condensed into a permanent checkpoint and linked to your commit by an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.
290:- **No commits on your branch** — Entire never creates commits on the active branch
291:- **Safe on any branch** — works on main, master, and feature branches alike
292:- **Metadata stored separately** — session data lives in per-checkpoint refs, never in your branch's history
300:Multiple AI sessions can run on the same commit. If you start a second session while another has uncommitted work, Entire warns you and tracks them separately. Both sessions' checkpoints are preserved, and a commit condenses every session with pending work in that worktree.
304:By default `entire login` opens a browser to sign in and stores tokens in the OS keyring (macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service, Windows Credential Manager). Machines without a usable browser or keyring — headless servers, containers, minimal VMs, CI runners — have two supported paths:
306:### Interactive login on a headless machine
308:Sign-in itself already handles this: with no interactive terminal, over SSH, or on a Linux or BSD machine with no graphical display, `entire login` switches to the device-code flow on its own and prints an approval URL you can open on any machine. `entire login --device` forces that flow explicitly. Only token *storage* needs an override — use the file-backed store:
311:ENTIRE_TOKEN_STORE=file entire login
318:Skip login and storage entirely by injecting a token per invocation:
321:ENTIRE_TOKEN=<login-or-sa-session-JWT> entire ...
326:> **Seeing `save login` / `failed to unlock correct collection` errors from `entire login`?** That's the OS keyring being unavailable — use one of the two paths above.
330:Descriptions below are the commands' own summaries. `entire help` always reflects the installed binary; `entire agent-help` is the machine-readable version agents read.
339:| `entire agent`     | Manage agent integrations (`add`, `remove`, `list`)                                |
340:| `entire configure` | Update non-agent Entire settings in the current repository                          |
341:| `entire doctor`    | Diagnose and fix session issues (`trace`, `logs`, `bundle`, `migrate-checkpoints`)  |
345:### Sessions & Checkpoints
349:| `entire session`              | Manage agent sessions (`list`, `info`, `current`, `stop`, `attach`, `adopt`, `resume`, `tokens`) |
350:| `entire session resume`       | Resume a stopped session — interactive picker, or by branch                               |
351:| `entire checkpoint`           | Inspect and search checkpoints (`list`, `explain`, `tokens`, `search`)                    |
352:| `entire checkpoint explain`   | Explain a checkpoint, commit, or session                                                 |
353:| `entire search`               | Search checkpoints, commits, and sessions using semantic and keyword matching            |
355:| `entire recap`                | Summarize recent checkpoint activity                                                     |
356:| `entire dispatch`             | Generate a dispatch summarizing recent agent work                                         |
362:| `entire login`   | Log in to Entire (browser by default; `--device` for the device-code flow)            |
364:| `entire auth`    | Manage authentication (`status`, `contexts`, `switch`, `token`, `login`, `logout`)       |
380:| `entire agent-help` | Machine-readable usage for coding agents (always matches the installed CLI)     |
390:| `entire review`      | Run a multi-agent review against a branch                |
391:| `entire tokens`      | Analyze token usage across sessions and checkpoints       |
392:| `entire blame`       | Show which lines came from Entire checkpoints             |
394:| `entire experts`     | Rank agent provenance for code scopes                    |
395:| `entire import`      | Import pre-existing agent history into Entire            |
398:`entire blame <file>` shows which current file lines came from an Entire checkpoint (`--long` for the full agent, model, author, and session table), and `entire why <file>:<line>` jumps from a specific line back to the prompt, session, and checkpoint that created it.
404:| `--agent <name>`                            | Agent to set up hooks for: `antigravity`, `claude-code`, `codex`, `copilot-cli`, `cursor`, `factoryai-droid`, `opencode`, `pi` (external agents on `$PATH` also work). Enables non-interactive mode |
407:| `--checkpoint-remote <provider:owner/repo>` | Push checkpoint data to a separate repo; providers `github`, `gitlab` (e.g., `github:org/checkpoints-repo`)      |
408:| `--checkpoint-push-remote <name>`           | Select an existing Git remote for checkpoints; always saves to this clone's `.entire/settings.local.json`, even with `--project` |
409:| `--skip-push-sessions`                      | Disable automatic pushing of checkpoint data on git push                                                           |
413:| `--import-history`                          | During first-time setup, import the selected agents' existing session history (last 30 days) without prompting     |
414:| `--search-skill`                            | Install the optional Entire search skill for the selected agent(s)                                                |
415:| `--agent-help-skill`                        | Install the Entire agent-help skill (points agents at `entire agent-help`) for the selected agent(s)              |

219:A **session** represents a complete interaction with your AI agent, from start to finish. Each session captures all prompts, responses, files modified, and timestamps.
221:The session ID is the unique identifier the agent itself provides — Entire never mints its own — so an ID you see in `entire session list` is the same one the agent uses. The format is the agent's to choose: most supply a UUID (e.g. `019efea2-b46a-7cbc-be01-4c13460f5019`), while OpenCode uses `ses_`-prefixed IDs.
223:Sessions are stored separately from your code commits, in the repo's checkpoint storage.
225:### Checkpoints
227:A **checkpoint** is a snapshot within a session—a "save point" in your work.
229:Checkpoints are created when you or the agent make a git commit, and the commit carries an `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` trailer linking the two.
231:**Checkpoint IDs** are 26-character ULIDs (e.g. `REDACTED`), which sort by creation time. Checkpoints written by older versions of Entire carry a legacy 12-character hex ID (e.g. `a3b2c4d5e6f7`); both formats stay readable in the same repo, and you can pass either to any command that takes a checkpoint ID.

235:Checkpoints live in your repository's own git object store, never in your branch's history. Each checkpoint is its own git ref:
238:refs/entire/checkpoints/<shard>/<id>
241:The ref points at a commit whose tree *is* that checkpoint — `metadata.json`, the per-session transcript files, and any subagent task records. `<shard>` is the last two characters of the ID, which keeps the refs evenly distributed.
243:Because checkpoints are independent refs, they are written, pushed, and fetched independently. There is no shared branch tip for concurrent sessions to contend on, and a reader can fetch exactly the one checkpoint it needs instead of a whole history. A checkpoint written on another machine is fetched on demand the first time you read it.

284:As you work, Entire tracks which files the agent touched (and their content hashes) in local session state, alongside a local copy of the transcript; nothing is written to git until you commit. When you commit, that work is condensed into a permanent checkpoint and linked to your commit by an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer.

## Security & Privacy

**Your session transcripts are stored in your git repository**, in the [per-checkpoint refs](#checkpoint-storage) described above. If your repository is public, this data is visible to anyone.

Entire automatically redacts detected secrets (API keys, tokens, credentials) from transcripts and metadata before writing a checkpoint, but redaction is best-effort.

Older Entire versions also kept local `entire/<commit>-<worktree>` shadow branches whose code-file snapshots were raw blobs of your working tree. Current versions no longer create them, but do not delete leftover ones automatically: `entire doctor` reports them and `entire doctor --force` deletes them, leaving pending agent work alone (plain `entire clean` would also clear the session state that records it). `entire disable --uninstall` deletes the `entire/<commit>-<worktree>` form too, and lists any oldest-form `entire/<commit>` branches without deleting them, since a branch of yours named after a short SHA looks the same; `entire clean --all` covers that form after you confirm. See [docs/security-and-privacy.md](docs/security-and-privacy.md) for the full picture, including the configurable scanner layers and opt-in PII redaction.

## Troubleshooting

# Security Policy

We take security seriously at Entire. We appreciate your efforts to responsibly disclose vulnerabilities and will make every effort to acknowledge your contributions.

## Reporting a Vulnerability

**Please do not report security vulnerabilities through public GitHub issues.**

Instead, please send security-related reports to **[security@entire.io](mailto:security@entire.io)**.

### What to Include

When reporting a vulnerability, please include:

1. **Description** - A clear description of the vulnerability
2. **Impact** - What an attacker could achieve by exploiting this issue
3. **Steps to reproduce** - Detailed steps to reproduce the vulnerability
4. **Affected versions** - Which versions of the CLI are affected (if known)
5. **Suggested fix** - If you have ideas on how to fix it (optional)

### What to Expect

- **Acknowledgment** - We will acknowledge receipt of your report within 48 hours
- **Updates** - We will keep you informed of our progress as we investigate
- **Resolution** - We aim to resolve critical vulnerabilities within 90 days

## Confidentiality

**All reports will be kept confidential.** We will not share your information with third parties without your consent, except as required by law.

## Supported Versions

We recommend always running the latest version of the Entire CLI.

## Scope

This security policy applies to:

- The Entire CLI (`entire` command-line tool)
- Official Entire GitHub repositories

# Security Policy
mise is a convenient tool to manage developer tools, however its model is also open to potential risks. The following
are major areas of mise and the security considerations currently being made and what needs to be made in the future.
Please open a ticket or send me an email if you have thoughts on how mise can be made more secure.
## Core CLI Security
Development of the "core CLI" is done on jdx/mise which only a single developer (me, @jdx) has access to.
Other contributors may only submit contributions via public Pull Requests. Reducing the number
of developers with access down to 1 minimizes the chance of keys being leaked.
This does create a [bus factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_factor) problem. If I suddenly died one day
or otherwise wasn't able to continue development at all there are some successors listed in my GitHub account
that can take over my account if need be.
The dependencies in the core CLI are a security vector. I've tried to be judicious about what dependencies make it into
the project. I only select dependencies with broad usage across the Rust community where possible.
I'm open to PRs or suggestions on reducing dependency count even at the cost of functionality because it will make
mise more secure.
## mise.jdx.dev
mise.jdx.dev is the asset host for mise. It's used to host precompiled mise CLI binaries, and hosts a "[VERSION](https://mise.jdx.dev/VERSION)"
which mise uses to occasionally check for a new version being released. Everything hosted there uses a single
vendor to reduce surface area.
## Download verification
mise verifies downloads itself, without external `cosign`, `slsa-verifier`,
`minisign`, `gpg` or `gh` executables. What it checks depends on the backend and
on what the upstream project publishes: checksums, Cosign and Minisign
signatures, SLSA provenance, GitHub artifact attestations, and signed packslip
release manifests. These checks are on by default, and a failed check aborts
the install. Run `mise tool <name>` to see which checks apply to a tool, and see
[Download verification](https://mise.jdx.dev/security.html#download-verification)
for the full table and the settings that control each check.
If a tool publishes signatures or provenance that mise does not check yet,
consider a PR that declares them, for example in the
[aqua registry](https://github.com/aquaproj/aqua-registry).
## `mise.lock`
A [lockfile](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/mise-lock.html) records the exact
version, artifact checksums and verified provenance of each tool. Commit it so
every developer and CI system installs the same artifacts. Not every backend
supports it; asdf plugins do not.
## asdf plugins
asdf plugins are dangerous. They are typically owned by developers unconnected
to either asdf or the tool vendor, and they may get hacked or inject malicious
code that runs on your machine.
The [registry](https://github.com/jdx/mise/blob/main/registry/) avoids asdf
plugins whenever a safer backend works, preferring packslip, aqua and GitHub
releases. The asdf plugins it still uses are hosted in the
[mise-plugins org](https://github.com/mise-plugins), so you do not rely on
plugins maintained by anyone except me. If you _manually_ add plugins from
elsewhere, make sure they come from a trusted source.
To help move tools off asdf plugins, check whether a tool works with the
packslip, aqua or github backend and submit a PR to
[registry/](https://github.com/jdx/mise/blob/main/registry/). New tools that use
asdf are **not** likely to be accepted unless no other backend can support them.

The only supported version is the most recent one.

# Security Policy
mise is a convenient tool to manage developer tools, however its model is also open to potential risks. The following
are major areas of mise and the security considerations currently being made and what needs to be made in the future.
Please open a ticket or send me an email if you have thoughts on how mise can be made more secure.
## Core CLI Security
Development of the "core CLI" is done on jdx/mise which only a single developer (me, @jdx) has access to.
Other contributors may only submit contributions via public Pull Requests. Reducing the number
of developers with access down to 1 minimizes the chance of keys being leaked.
This does create a [bus factor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bus_factor) problem. If I suddenly died one day
or otherwise wasn't able to continue development at all there are some successors listed in my GitHub account
that can take over my account if need be.
The dependencies in the core CLI are a security vector. I've tried to be judicious about what dependencies make it into
the project. I only select dependencies with broad usage across the Rust community where possible.
I'm open to PRs or suggestions on reducing dependency count even at the cost of functionality because it will make
mise more secure.
## mise.jdx.dev
mise.jdx.dev is the asset host for mise. It's used to host precompiled mise CLI binaries, and hosts a "[VERSION](https://mise.jdx.dev/VERSION)"
which mise uses to occasionally check for a new version being released. Everything hosted there uses a single
vendor to reduce surface area.
## Download verification
mise verifies downloads itself, without external `cosign`, `slsa-verifier`,
`minisign`, `gpg` or `gh` executables. What it checks depends on the backend and
on what the upstream project publishes: checksums, Cosign and Minisign
signatures, SLSA provenance, GitHub artifact attestations, and signed packslip
release manifests. These checks are on by default, and a failed check aborts
the install. Run `mise tool <name>` to see which checks apply to a tool, and see
[Download verification](https://mise.jdx.dev/security.html#download-verification)
for the full table and the settings that control each check.
If a tool publishes signatures or provenance that mise does not check yet,
consider a PR that declares them, for example in the
[aqua registry](https://github.com/aquaproj/aqua-registry).
## `mise.lock`
A [lockfile](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/mise-lock.html) records the exact
version, artifact checksums and verified provenance of each tool. Commit it so
every developer and CI system installs the same artifacts. Not every backend
supports it; asdf plugins do not.
## asdf plugins
asdf plugins are dangerous. They are typically owned by developers unconnected
to either asdf or the tool vendor, and they may get hacked or inject malicious
code that runs on your machine.
The [registry](https://github.com/jdx/mise/blob/main/registry/) avoids asdf
plugins whenever a safer backend works, preferring packslip, aqua and GitHub
releases. The asdf plugins it still uses are hosted in the
[mise-plugins org](https://github.com/mise-plugins), so you do not rely on
plugins maintained by anyone except me. If you _manually_ add plugins from
elsewhere, make sure they come from a trusted source.
To help move tools off asdf plugins, check whether a tool works with the
packslip, aqua or github backend and submit a PR to
[registry/](https://github.com/jdx/mise/blob/main/registry/). New tools that use
asdf are **not** likely to be accepted unless no other backend can support them.

content.content:
**Summary of the Entire Inc. Privacy Policy (last updated 06 July 2026)**

**Data collected**
- **Personal information:** name and email, provided directly or through sign-in providers such as GitHub, Google, Microsoft, and SSO.
- **Usage data:** IP address, device identifiers, browser details, pages visited, and diagnostic data, collected automatically.
- **Cookies and tracking:** essential, functional, and tracking/performance cookies. Non-essential cookies require consent where the law requires it.
- **Imported content:** repository files, commit messages and metadata, and issue and pull request content from sources like GitHub. This can include personal information about other people, such as commit authors and reviewers.

The policy does not specifically mention CLI telemetry or AI session transcripts. "Chat transcripts" appear only in the customer support context.

**Subprocessors**
- PostHog (analytics)
- Honeycomb and Datadog (monitoring)
- HubSpot (sales and marketing communications)
- WorkOS (authentication and SSO)

Cloud providers are not named. The policy refers only to "service providers" in general.

**Data location**
The policy says it "aims to store and process your personal information within your own jurisdiction." Where processing happens elsewhere, it says appropriate safeguards apply. For EEA and UK residents, it describes Standard Contractual Clauses, the UK IDTA, and the UK Addendum as safeguards for international transfers.

**AI model training**
The policy does not mention using data for AI model training. It does say anonymized data may be retained indefinitely for "research and analytics."

**Retention**
- **Repository content:** kept "for as long as the relevant repository exists on our services."
- **User accounts:** kept for the account relationship plus up to 24 months after closure.
- **Support tickets and chat transcripts:** up to 24 months.
- **Analytics and server logs:** up to 24 months.

**User rights**
- **Access and correction:** available through account settings or by contacting the company, and under CCPA/CPRA.
- **Deletion:** available on request. Repository history may not be deletable while the repository exists.
- **Portability/export:** under GDPR, users can receive their data "in a structured, commonly used, machine-readable format." The policy does not describe a general export feature.
- **Other GDPR rights:** restriction, objection, withdrawal of consent, and complaints to a data protection authority.

**Canada and PIPEDA**
The policy does not mention Canada or PIPEDA. It covers GDPR/UK GDPR, CCPA/CPRA, and several other US state laws.

**Entity and governing law**
- The provider is **Entire Inc**, "registered in the State of Delaware, United States."
- Delaware law governs: "The laws of the State of Delaware, United States, excluding its conflicts of law rules, shall govern these Terms." EU consumers keep the mandatory protections of their country of residence.

**Your content, code, and data**
- You keep ownership. You grant Entire a "non-exclusive, worldwide, royalty-free license" to host, store, parse, reproduce, display, modify, and transmit your content, "as necessary to operate, provide, and improve our services."
- Imported content from third-party sources (for example, a code host) gets the same license once you authorize the integration.
- **AI training:** Entire may use your content to run AI features you invoke, such as summarization or search. It states it does not use your content to train generative AI models for general use outside its services. Any other AI training "requires your separate, affirmative opt-in."
- **Private repositories:** Entire says it treats them as confidential and accesses them only for listed purposes, such as security scanning, support you request, or legal compliance.
- **Session data:** The terms don't mention session data specifically. The referenced Privacy Policy and Data Processing Agreement, which would cover it, weren't included.

**Changes to the terms**
- Entire "may modify these Terms at any time," and continued use counts as acceptance. The section summary mentions 30 days' notice for material changes, but the operative text sets no notice period.

**Termination**
- Entire may suspend or terminate "immediately, without prior notice" for material breach or where continued service is likely to cause harm. Otherwise it must give reasonable notice.
- You can terminate at any time. Your right to use the service then ends immediately.

**Data export and deletion**
- Unless termination results from your material breach or retention is prohibited by law, Entire must give you at least 30 days to export your content.

- Entire says it doesn't guarantee backups are free of data loss or corruption, so the terms advise keeping your own independent copy.

**Fees**
- The terms don't describe any pricing or fees. They only refer to amounts "actually paid by you," which sets the liability cap: the amount you paid, or 100 USD if you haven't purchased anything.

content.content:
## Decision

- Code is licensed under the MIT License, SPDX identifier `MIT`.
- Documentation and content are licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International, `CC-BY-4.0`. There is no longer a separate share-alike licence for documentation.
- Licences are still marked with REUSE: `LICENSES/MIT.txt` and `LICENSES/CC-BY-4.0.txt`, `REUSE.toml` by path, and a per-file SPDX identifier only where a file differs. A document's `dc:rights` matches the licence that covers it.
- Every repository keeps a root `LICENSE`, holding the MIT text, byte-identical to `LICENSES/MIT.txt`. The MIT text carries its copyright line filled in, `Copyright (c) 2026 Christopher Steel`, in both, so both come from one payload, the `license-mit` offering.
- Contributions are accepted under the same licences: inbound equals outbound.
- The `license-gpl-3-0-or-later` and `license-cc-by-sa-4-0` offerings are withdrawn; `license-mit` and `license-cc-by-4-0` take their place, and the base layout requires both.

## Consequences

- uc-automa 0001 and 0021 are superseded; they stay as the record of the earlier decision.
- The three repositories' commit histories, before their first public release, contain work marked GPL-3.0-or-later and CC-BY-SA-4.0, all by Christopher Steel as sole author. Releases are MIT and CC BY 4.0 from 0.1.0.
- Marking the Universal Cake name and logo as excluded from the licences waits for the trademark policy to be published.

# Radar

The radar is a register of things under consideration for SAT — tools, protocols, apps, and techniques — before they settle into the documentation proper. It is a triage space, not a home. An entry sits on the radar only while its fate is undecided.

## Rings

The radar has three rings, each a directory:

- **assess/** — under evaluation; we are looking at it and weighing its fit
- **adopt/** — accepted; the decision is yes
- **hold/** — rejected, or not now

The ring is the decision. An entry's location states the verdict; no separate decision record is kept.

## Adoption graduates out

`adopt/` is a transit state, not storage. Once an entry is adopted its idea moves to its permanent home elsewhere in `en/docs/` — `language/`, `architecture/`, `guides/`, `specifications/`, and so on — and the radar entry leaves. The radar holds only what is still in question, so a healthy `adopt/` is often empty.

## Categories

The radar has no category subdirectories. What kind of thing an entry is lives in its `Category` field (see the entry template), and is ultimately expressed by where it graduates to. Rings classify the decision; the category and destination classify the kind.

## What this radar omits

This radar departs deliberately from the conventional four-ring model:

- **No `trial` ring.** Trial marks piloting between assessment and adoption. SAT has no such stage — an item is under assessment, adopted, or held, and `assess` covers the gap.
- **No `decisions/` folder.** The ring already records the decision and git records its history; a separate log would duplicate both.

## Rationale travels with the entry

Nothing moves to `adopt/` or `hold/` without a status note stating why. The verdict is the folder, the reasoning is in the entry, the history is git. When an entry graduates, its rationale travels into the destination document rather than being left behind.

## File naming

Radar entries diverge from the SAT file-naming convention. An entry filename is its slug joined to a short tagline by a double hyphen, with no version suffix:

```text
dual-mode-language-authority--standard-aware-not-standard-dependent.md
```

The double hyphen separates the blip slug from its tagline so an entry can be identified on the radar without opening it. Versions are not suffixed; revision history lives in git. This is a deliberate local override of the File Naming rule in the documentation style guide.

## Entry template

New entries are based on `radar-entry-template.md` in this directory.

# osat-manager-git

This project builds `manage-git`, which installs git into a user's own account on Linux, macOS and Windows, keeps several versions side by side, and tells other managers whether git meets a baseline contract. It follows [Creating an OSAT Manager Repository](../../docs/guides/new-repository/creating-an-osat-manager-repository-v0.4.0.md), version 0.4.0, stage by stage. It is the second manager built that way, after osat-manager-restic.

Status: Planned. Drafted with AI assistance (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) on 2026-10-21 and provisional until Christopher Steel confirms it.

## Where things stand

- **The earlier scoping.** The checkout at `osat-manager-git/` has no commits. It holds two drafts from 2026-09-30, a process overview and *Universal Cake Requirements: Add Document Slice*. Their baseline contract, the requirement areas (ID, ML, SEC, AL, GIT) and en-ca and fr-ca messages still stand. Their build sequence does not: installing through apt, dnf, Homebrew and winget breaks the manager contract, which allows no system package manager and no elevated privilege.
- **Windows.** The radar entry *Git on Windows, Options for osat-manager-git* (uc-radar, 2026-10-11) recommends MinGit from Git for Windows releases for Trial, with four decisions to make first: line endings, Git LFS, inherited system configuration and paths.
- **Linux and macOS.** That entry left dugite-native as the candidate. It needs glibc 2.34, links the system's libcurl, and repackages builds made for GitHub Desktop. This plan proposes conda-forge instead, as recommended on 2026-10-21.
- **Prior art.** mise's conda backend already installs conda-forge packages without conda, solving, verifying and relocating them through the rattler library. See the radar entry *Universal Cake Evaluation: mise-en-place*, drafted alongside this plan.

## Sources proposed

| Platform | Source | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux, x86_64 and aarch64 | conda-forge `git`, subdirs `linux-64` and `linux-aarch64` | Built from the kernel.org source tarball, with its SHA-256 pinned in the recipe. Needs glibc 2.17 or later, so it runs on far older systems than dugite-native |
| macOS, x86_64 and arm64 | conda-forge `git`, subdirs `osx-64` and `osx-arm64` | Same recipe; needs macOS 11 or later |
| Windows, x64 and ARM64 | MinGit, from Git for Windows releases | conda-forge's `win-64` git is PortableGit repackaged. It is 121 MB with Git Bash, and was built from `v2.56.0.windows.1` while Git for Windows is at `.windows.2`. It adds a link to the chain and nothing else |

The principle generalizes to later managers: take upstream's own signed binaries when they exist, as restic and Git for Windows publish them, and use conda-forge when upstream publishes no portable binaries, as git does for Linux and macOS.

## What conda-forge publishes for git

Read from the anaconda.org API and from `linux-64/git-2.56.0-pl5440h3795e67_0.conda`, downloaded and unpacked on 2026-10-21. Nothing was run.

- **Version.** 2.56.0, build 0, uploaded 2026-09-29 for `linux-64`, `linux-aarch64`, `linux-ppc64le`, `linux-riscv64`, `osx-64`, `osx-arm64`, `win-64` and `win-arm64`.
- **Format.** A `.conda` file: a zip holding `pkg-…tar.zst` and `info-…tar.zst`. Recent builds come in this format only. Python's standard library reads zstd only from 3.14, through `compression.zstd`.
- **Dependencies.** On `linux-64`, nine direct runtime dependencies: `__glibc >=2.17`, `libcurl`, `libexpat`, `libgcc`, `libiconv`, `libzlib`, `openssl`, `pcre2` and `perl 5.*`. More come in transitively (krb5, libssh2, libnghttp2, c-ares, zstd and others; not counted). macOS adds `libintl`. `win-64` declares none.
- **Relocation.** `info/has_prefix` lists 32 files that contain the build prefix, 19 text and 13 binary, among them `bin/git` and `bin/git-shell`. They must be rewritten for the install location, and binary placeholders padded with null bytes. On macOS arm64, a patched binary must be re-signed ad hoc or it will not run.
- **Verification.** Each file's SHA-256 and MD5 are published in the channel's repodata and API, over HTTPS. The packages carry no signature. Whether conda-forge publishes Sigstore attestations under CEP 27, which prefix.dev's channels support in public beta, was not established.
- **Licence metadata.** The recipe labels git `GPL-2.0-or-later and LGPL-2.1-or-later`. Git is GPL-2.0-only, as the Windows entry verified from Git's own `COPYING`. `manager.yaml` records `GPL-2.0-only`, and the mislabel is worth reporting to the git-feedstock.

## What manage-git needs that manage-restic does not

1. **Reading zstd.** See decision D1 below.
2. **A fixed set of packages.** The manager cannot solve dependencies at runtime and still stay small and reviewable. It is resolved when the manager is released instead. For each git version and platform, a lock file records every package's URL, SHA-256 and size. The manager installs exactly that set into one prefix per version.
3. **Relocation.** The manager rewrites text and binary prefix placeholders in the standard library, following `info/paths.json`, and refuses any package whose `paths.json` it does not fully understand.
4. **Re-signing on macOS.** On arm64, the patched Mach-O files need an ad hoc signature. That means either running `/usr/bin/codesign`, which breaks the no-shell-commands rule, or writing a signature in Python. This is the riskiest item in the plan.
5. **A weaker trust anchor.** restic and MinGit give a signed checksum list or a signed tag. conda-forge gives hashes served over HTTPS. The lock file becomes the trust anchor, reviewed when it changes and signed with the release key (uc-automa 0032).
6. **CA certificates.** conda's `openssl` and `libcurl` look for certificates inside the prefix, so `ca-certificates` must be in the lock. Otherwise HTTPS clones fail.
7. **System configuration.** The prefix's `etc/gitconfig` belongs to the manager, which writes the baseline settings there: line endings, `safe.directory`, credential helper, and long paths on Windows. It never inherits configuration from another install, the problem the Windows entry found with MinGit.
8. **Two source kinds in one manager.** Conda packages on Linux and macOS, a zip with a SHA-256 table from release notes on Windows. Both go in `manager.yaml`, with platform differences kept in one module.

## Decisions needed from Christopher Steel

Each has a recommendation, so the project can start once these are confirmed or changed.

| ID | Question | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D1 | How does a standard-library manager read zstd? | Require Python 3.14 or later for manage-git, since manage-python installs it, and use `compression.zstd`. Record this in decision 0001 as a difference from the contract. The alternative is a pure-Python zstd decoder: new, security-critical code that would need independent review, as the OpenPGP verifier did |
| D2 | What anchors trust in conda-forge packages? | A per-version lock file, reviewed and released with the manager and signed with the release key. Check attestations under CEP 27 too, if conda-forge publishes them, and make them required once they are available for every platform |
| D3 | Where does the conda logic live? | In the shared manager package (uc-automa 0024), as a `conda-forge` source kind, so later managers for git-lfs, gh, pandoc, rclone and others differ only in `manager.yaml`. That means building the shared package first, which 0024 already calls for |
| D4 | How does macOS arm64 re-signing work? | Allow one named exception, `/usr/bin/codesign -s - -f` on files the manager has just patched, and record it in 0001. Revisit if a standard-library ad hoc signer proves small enough to review |
| D5 | Windows source | MinGit from Git for Windows, as the radar entry recommends, not conda-forge's `win-64` package |

## Before starting

- [ ] Confirm D1 to D5, or record the changed answers.
- [ ] Change this project's status to Active and fill `date_started`.

## Steps

The stages are those of the process guide. Each ends at its gate.

### 1. Assess on the radar

- [ ] Write a uc-radar entry for conda-forge as a binary source for OSAT managers, with git as the worked case. It answers the five questions the process asks, from the facts above.
- [ ] Add the Linux and macOS half to the git decision, replacing dugite-native, or record why dugite-native stays.
- [ ] Gate: MinGit and conda-forge git are each in Trial, or the entry says why a manager is still wanted.

### 2. Record the decision

- [ ] Draft `0001--build-manage-git-v0.1.0.md` outside the repository, in a hand-off folder. It names the tool, both radar entries, the platforms targeted first (Linux x86_64 and aarch64, macOS x86_64 and arm64, Windows x64), and every difference from the contract: D1, D4, and the two source kinds.
- [ ] Carry over the baseline contract and the requirement areas from the 2026-09-30 drafts; the drafts themselves go to the hand-off folder, not into the first commit.
- [ ] Gate: the decision record is drafted.

### 3. Build the shared package first (D3)

- [ ] Choose its name and repository, the open consequence of uc-automa 0024.
- [ ] Move in from osat-manager-restic the YAML subset reader, the data lookup (uc-automa 0019) and the OpenPGP verifier.
- [ ] Add the `conda-forge` source kind: read a lock, download, check SHA-256 and size, unpack `.conda`, relocate through `paths.json`, and re-sign on macOS arm64.
- [ ] Unit tests offline, against small fake `.conda` packages built in the tests, including placeholders longer than the install path, which must be refused.
- [ ] Independent review of the relocation and re-signing code before any manager depending on it is tagged.

### 4. Create the repository

- [ ] Clear out or archive the current `osat-manager-git/` checkout. Its first commit must hold only the sidecar and the decision record, so the existing drafts move out first. Christopher Steel decides where they go.
- [ ] `git init`, `uuidgen -r`, write `.osat-manager-git.assets/archive.yaml` and `dc.yaml`, and place the decision record.
- [ ] Gate: the first commit holds the sidecar and the decision record, and nothing else.

### 5. Subscribe to uc-automa

- [ ] Install uc-automa and uc-portage from their release tags, `uc-automa init --repository osat-manager-git --layout osat-manager`, `offerings plan`, `offerings apply`, commit.
- [ ] Gate: `uc-automa offerings plan` reports nothing to do.

- [ ] Write `manager.yaml`, covering the conda-forge channel and subdirs, the lock file per version, MinGit's release URL and SHA-256 table, the licence `GPL-2.0-only`, aliases `git` and `git-{major}.{minor}`, and install roots under `osat/git`.

# osat-manager-git

This project builds `manage-git`, which installs git into a user's own account on Linux, macOS and Windows, keeps several versions side by side, and tells other managers whether git meets a baseline contract. It follows [Creating an OSAT Manager Repository](../../docs/guides/new-repository/creating-an-osat-manager-repository-v0.4.0.md), version 0.4.0, stage by stage. It is the second manager built that way, after osat-manager-restic.

Status: Planned. Drafted with AI assistance (Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic) on 2026-10-21 and provisional until Christopher Steel confirms it.

## Where things stand

- **The earlier scoping.** The checkout at `osat-manager-git/` has no commits. It holds two drafts from 2026-09-30, a process overview and *Universal Cake Requirements: Add Document Slice*. Their baseline contract, the requirement areas (ID, ML, SEC, AL, GIT) and en-ca and fr-ca messages still stand. Their build sequence does not: installing through apt, dnf, Homebrew and winget breaks the manager contract, which allows no system package manager and no elevated privilege.
- **Windows.** The radar entry *Git on Windows, Options for osat-manager-git* (uc-radar, 2026-10-11) recommends MinGit from Git for Windows releases for Trial, with four decisions to make first: line endings, Git LFS, inherited system configuration and paths.
- **Linux and macOS.** That entry left dugite-native as the candidate. It needs glibc 2.34, links the system's libcurl, and repackages builds made for GitHub Desktop. This plan proposes conda-forge instead, as recommended on 2026-10-21.
- **Prior art.** mise's conda backend already installs conda-forge packages without conda, solving, verifying and relocating them through the rattler library. See the radar entry *Universal Cake Evaluation: mise-en-place*, drafted alongside this plan.

## Sources proposed

| Platform | Source | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linux, x86_64 and aarch64 | conda-forge `git`, subdirs `linux-64` and `linux-aarch64` | Built from the kernel.org source tarball, with its SHA-256 pinned in the recipe. Needs glibc 2.17 or later, so it runs on far older systems than dugite-native |
| macOS, x86_64 and arm64 | conda-forge `git`, subdirs `osx-64` and `osx-arm64` | Same recipe; needs macOS 11 or later |
| Windows, x64 and ARM64 | MinGit, from Git for Windows releases | conda-forge's `win-64` git is PortableGit repackaged. It is 121 MB with Git Bash, and was built from `v2.56.0.windows.1` while Git for Windows is at `.windows.2`. It adds a link to the chain and nothing else |

The principle generalizes to later managers: take upstream's own signed binaries when they exist, as restic and Git for Windows publish them, and use conda-forge when upstream publishes no portable binaries, as git does for Linux and macOS.

## What conda-forge publishes for git

Read from the anaconda.org API and from `linux-64/git-2.56.0-pl5440h3795e67_0.conda`, downloaded and unpacked on 2026-10-21. Nothing was run.

- **Version.** 2.56.0, build 0, uploaded 2026-09-29 for `linux-64`, `linux-aarch64`, `linux-ppc64le`, `linux-riscv64`, `osx-64`, `osx-arm64`, `win-64` and `win-arm64`.
- **Format.** A `.conda` file: a zip holding `pkg-…tar.zst` and `info-…tar.zst`. Recent builds come in this format only. Python's standard library reads zstd only from 3.14, through `compression.zstd`.
- **Dependencies.** On `linux-64`, nine direct runtime dependencies: `__glibc >=2.17`, `libcurl`, `libexpat`, `libgcc`, `libiconv`, `libzlib`, `openssl`, `pcre2` and `perl 5.*`. More come in transitively (krb5, libssh2, libnghttp2, c-ares, zstd and others; not counted). macOS adds `libintl`. `win-64` declares none.
- **Relocation.** `info/has_prefix` lists 32 files that contain the build prefix, 19 text and 13 binary, among them `bin/git` and `bin/git-shell`. They must be rewritten for the install location, and binary placeholders padded with null bytes. On macOS arm64, a patched binary must be re-signed ad hoc or it will not run.
- **Verification.** Each file's SHA-256 and MD5 are published in the channel's repodata and API, over HTTPS. The packages carry no signature. Whether conda-forge publishes Sigstore attestations under CEP 27, which prefix.dev's channels support in public beta, was not established.
- **Licence metadata.** The recipe labels git `GPL-2.0-or-later and LGPL-2.1-or-later`. Git is GPL-2.0-only, as the Windows entry verified from Git's own `COPYING`. `manager.yaml` records `GPL-2.0-only`, and the mislabel is worth reporting to the git-feedstock.

1. **Reading zstd.** See decision D1 below.
2. **A fixed set of packages.** The manager cannot solve dependencies at runtime and still stay small and reviewable. It is resolved when the manager is released instead. 3. **Relocation.** The manager rewrites text and binary prefix placeholders in the standard library, following `info/paths.json`, and refuses any package whose `paths.json` it does not fully understand.

5. **A weaker trust anchor.** restic and MinGit give a signed checksum list or a signed tag. conda-forge gives hashes served over HTTPS. The lock file becomes the trust anchor, reviewed when it changes and signed with the release key (uc-automa 0032).
6. **CA certificates.** conda's `openssl` and `libcurl` look for certificates inside the prefix, so `ca-certificates` must be in the lock. Otherwise HTTPS clones fail.
7. **System configuration.** The prefix's `etc/gitconfig` belongs to the manager, which writes the baseline settings there: line endings, `safe.directory`, credential helper, and long paths on Windows. Each has a recommendation, so the project can start once these are confirmed or changed.

| --- | --- | --- |

- **Licence metadata.** The recipe labels git `GPL-2.0-or-later and LGPL-2.1-or-later`. Git is GPL-2.0-only, as the Windows entry verified from Git's own `COPYING`. `manager.yaml` records `GPL-2.0-only`, and the mislabel is worth reporting to the git-feedstock.

## What manage-git needs that manage-restic does not

1. **Reading zstd.** See decision D1 below.
2. **A fixed set of packages.** The manager cannot solve dependencies at runtime and still stay small and reviewable. It is resolved when the manager is released instead. For each git version and platform, a lock file records every package's URL, SHA-256 and size. The manager installs exactly that set into one prefix per version.
3. **Relocation.** The manager rewrites text and binary prefix placeholders in the standard library, following `info/paths.json`, and refuses any package whose `paths.json` it does not fully understand.
4. **Re-signing on macOS.** On arm64, the patched Mach-O files need an ad hoc signature. That means either running `/usr/bin/codesign`, which breaks the no-shell-commands rule, or writing a signature in Python. This is the riskiest item in the plan.
5. **A weaker trust anchor.** restic and MinGit give a signed checksum list or a signed tag. conda-forge gives hashes served over HTTPS. The lock file becomes the trust anchor, reviewed when it changes and signed with the release key (uc-automa 0032).
6. **CA certificates.** conda's `openssl` and `libcurl` look for certificates inside the prefix, so `ca-certificates` must be in the lock. Otherwise HTTPS clones fail.
7. **System configuration.** The prefix's `etc/gitconfig` belongs to the manager, which writes the baseline settings there: line endings, `safe.directory`, credential helper, and long paths on Windows. It never inherits configuration from another install, the problem the Windows entry found with MinGit.
8. **Two source kinds in one manager.** Conda packages on Linux and macOS, a zip with a SHA-256 table from release notes on Windows. Both go in `manager.yaml`, with platform differences kept in one module.

## Decisions needed from Christopher Steel

Each has a recommendation, so the project can start once these are confirmed or changed.

| ID | Question | Recommendation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D1 | How does a standard-library manager read zstd? | Require Python 3.14 or later for manage-git, since manage-python installs it, and use `compression.zstd`. Record this in decision 0001 as a difference from the contract. The alternative is a pure-Python zstd decoder: new, security-critical code that would need independent review, as the OpenPGP verifier did |
| D2 | What anchors trust in conda-forge packages? | A per-version lock file, reviewed and released with the manager and signed with the release key. Check attestations under CEP 27 too, if conda-forge publishes them, and make them required once they are available for every platform |
| D3 | Where does the conda logic live? | In the shared manager package (uc-automa 0024), as a `conda-forge` source kind, so later managers for git-lfs, gh, pandoc, rclone and others differ only in `manager.yaml`. That means building the shared package first, which 0024 already calls for |
| D4 | How does macOS arm64 re-signing work? | Allow one named exception, `/usr/bin/codesign -s - -f` on files the manager has just patched, and record it in 0001. Revisit if a standard-library ad hoc signer proves small enough to review |
| D5 | Windows source | MinGit from Git for Windows, as the radar entry recommends, not conda-forge's `win-64` package |

## Risks

- macOS arm64 re-signing may not be doable in the standard library at a size worth reviewing, which leaves D4's exception in place.
- A transitive dependency's build can change under the same version, so a lock is valid only for the exact builds it names. Refreshing it is a reviewed change.
- conda-forge's git lags upstream by days to weeks. A security fix reaches users only after the feedstock rebuilds and the lock is refreshed.
- Perl comes with git on Linux and macOS, about as large again as git itself. Dropping it would break `git send-email`, `git svn` and other Perl commands.
- If conda-forge ends anonymous access to anaconda.org or changes the `.conda` format, the verified archive still restores installed versions offline, but new versions stop until the source changes.

Its risks are a single maintainer with write access to the core and a registry that still leans on asdf plugins for some tools. We recommend keeping it in Assess, studying its conda backend while osat-manager-git is designed, and allowing a workstation trial under the conditions below. ## Sources and Acknowledgements The evaluation applies *Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics* version 0.5.1 ([Steel, 2026](#apa-uc-metrics-reference)). The evaluation was prepared with AI assistance from Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic). ## Scope We evaluate mise v2026.10.17, released on 2026-10-21, as a developer tool on a person's own machine and as a design reference for OSAT managers. Its task runner and environment features are described but not rated in depth. Tools that mise installs are out of scope; each needs its own entry. ## Scorecard metadata - Product or service name: mise-en-place (mise) - Version evaluated: v2026.10.17; repository `jdx/mise` as of 2026-10-21 - Evaluator: Christopher Steel, with AI assistance from Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic) - Date: 2026-10-21 - Radar ring: Assess - Test platform: none; documents, source and release metadata only ## Gates | Gate | Result | Evidence | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | Telemetry or content exposure that cannot be disabled | Pass | Inferred | The security policy names one regular contact, an occasional check of `mise.jdx.dev/VERSION` for a new release. Calendar versioning, so stability is judged per change rather than by major version | | Gates | Pass | Mixed | All four pass; licence Verified, the others Inferred | ## Findings ### The conda backend, and why it matters for OSAT mise can install packages from conda-forge with no conda, mamba or micromamba on the machine ([mise Project, n.d.-a](#apa-mise-conda-docs-reference)). It picks the host's subdir (`linux-64`, `linux-aarch64`, `osx-64`, `osx-arm64` or `win-64`), solves the package and its dependencies from a single channel into one isolated prefix per tool, and puts only the requested package's commands on `PATH`. The source shows it uses rattler, prefix.dev's Rust conda library, for solving, extraction and linking. Linking rewrites text and binary prefix placeholders and re-signs on macOS. Each download is checked against the SHA-256 from repodata, and a locked install takes every package URL and checksum from `mise.lock` rather than solving again ([mise Project, n.d.-c](#apa-mise-conda-src-reference)). That list is the work osat-manager-git has to do on Linux and macOS, so mise is the closest working reference. It shows that the approach works in practice, and in which order the steps go: lock, download, verify, extract, relocate, re-sign. It also shows the hard parts: packages from more than one channel are not supported, and the host still supplies native requirements such as glibc. The backend left experimental status in release 2026.5.0 (claimed, from a mirror of the release notes). mise is not a candidate dependency for OSAT managers, which are standard-library Python by contract. That limits who could leak keys, and it creates a bus factor of one, which the policy acknowledges and answers with named successors on the author's GitHub account. For a workstation tool this is acceptable with the lock file in use. For anything a client depends on, it is a reason to prefer OSAT managers. ### asdf plugins The registry prefers packslip, aqua and GitHub release backends, and keeps the remaining asdf plugins in an organization the author controls. asdf plugins run arbitrary shell code from third parties at install time, and `mise.lock` does not cover them. Anyone trialling mise should avoid tools that resolve to an asdf plugin; `mise tool ` shows which backend and checks apply. ## Recommendation Keep mise in Assess. - **For OSAT.** Use its conda backend as the reference design for osat-manager-git on Linux and macOS, and cite it in that manager's decision record. This was read, not tested. ### Maintainer concentration The policy states plainly that only the author has write access to the core repository. That limits who could leak keys, and it creates a bus factor of one, which the policy acknowledges and answers with named successors on the author's GitHub account. For a workstation tool this is acceptable with the lock file in use. For anything a client depends on, it is a reason to prefer OSAT managers. ### asdf plugins The registry prefers packslip, aqua and GitHub release backends, and keeps the remaining asdf plugins in an organization the author controls. asdf plugins run arbitrary shell code from third parties at install time, and `mise.lock` does not cover them. Anyone trialling mise should avoid tools that resolve to an asdf plugin; `mise tool ` shows which backend and checks apply. ## Recommendation Keep mise in Assess. - **For OSAT.** Use its conda backend as the reference design for osat-manager-git on Linux and macOS, and cite it in that manager's decision record. It offers an open-source command-line tool that records each agent session and links it to the git commits it produced, plus a growing set of hosted services: a Git hosting network, session storage, and search across code, commits and sessions. This entry evaluates every product and service listed on entire.io on 2026-10-21. The CLI's design is good for sovereignty, because the records live in the repository's own git objects, not in a vendor's database. Its defaults are not: transcripts are pushed wherever the code is pushed, and usage analytics are on. The hosted services cannot yet be recommended for client or Universal Cake data. We recommend Assess for the CLI, with a private trial possible under conditions, and no hosted use until the conditions under Recommendation change. ## Sources and Acknowledgements The evaluation applies *Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics* version 0.5.1 ([Steel, 2026](#apa-uc-metrics-reference)). Product facts come from the entire.io home page ([Entire Inc., n.d.-a](#apa-entire-home-reference)), its terms of service ([Entire Inc., n.d.-c](#apa-entire-terms-reference)) and privacy policy, last updated 2026-07-06 ([Entire Inc., n.d.-b](#apa-entire-privacy-reference)), the `entireio/cli` README and security policy ([Entire Inc., n.d.-d](#apa-entire-readme-reference)), and the GitHub API's description of the `entireio/cli` and `entireio/entire-graph` repositories and their latest releases, all read on 2026-10-21. Funding and launch details come from Entire's announcement and trade press, and are tagged Claimed. Nothing was installed or run. The evaluation was prepared with AI assistance from Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic). ## Scope The subject is Entire's offering as listed on entire.io on 2026-10-21. The CLI is rated in most depth, since it is the only part that can be inspected. Hosted services are rated from their terms, privacy policy and public claims. The AI agents that Entire records, such as Claude Code, are out of scope. ## What Entire offers | Product or service | What it is | Form | Licence or terms | Evidence | |---|---|---|---|---| | Entire CLI (`entire`), with Checkpoints | Hooks into git and supported agents; records each session's transcript, prompts, files touched and token use, and links it to commits through an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer. Adds `entire blame`, `entire why`, session resume, search, recaps and multi-agent review | Local binary for Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64; v0.12.0, released 2026-10-21 | MIT | Verified from the repository and release | | Supported agents | `antigravity`, `claude-code`, `codex`, `copilot-cli`, `cursor`, `factoryai-droid`, `opencode`, `pi`, and external agents on `PATH` | | | Verified from the README | | `git-remote-entire` | A git remote helper for cloning over `entire://` | Local binary, installed with the CLI | MIT | Verified from the README | | entire-graph | A precomputed map of a repository for agents: ranked code search, definitions, callers, types, routes and change impact; runs locally | Local binary; only nightly releases so far, latest `v0.4.1-nightly`, 2026-09-03 | MIT | Verified from the repository | | forgemark | An open-source git hosting benchmark, used for Entire's speed claims | Source repository | Not established | Claimed by the site | | Git hosting | "The fastest Git network on Earth": hosted repositories, mirrored globally; the site claims agents clone and push up to 89 times faster than competitors, from its own benchmark | Hosted | Terms of service | Claimed | | Multi-region hosting | Code resident in a chosen region: India, Australia, the EU and the US today; "decentralized everywhere" marked soon | Hosted | Terms of service | Claimed | | Session storage | Sessions linked to commits, with secrets detected and redacted before storage | Hosted, and in the repository through the CLI | Terms of service | Claimed | | Agentic Search | One query across repositories, commits and agent sessions | Hosted | Terms of service | Claimed | | Rebellion | A mailing list and community: news, early access, releases | Email list | Not established | Claimed | No pricing is published: `entire.io/pricing` returned 404 on 2026-10-21, and the home page's only call to action is a sign-in. Both `entire.io` and `entire.com` serve the site, and the README's install script uses `entire.com`. ## Gates | Gate | Result | Evidence | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | Telemetry or content exposure that cannot be disabled | Pass, with conditions | Verified | Usage analytics go to PostHog by default and can be switched off with `entire configure --telemetry=false`. Transcripts are pushed with every `git push` by default; `--skip-push-sessions` or `strategy_options.push_sessions: false` stops that, and `--checkpoint-remote` sends them to a separate repository instead. Both can be disabled, so the gate passes, but both defaults expose content | | A licence incompatible with the project | Pass, CLI and entire-graph | Verified | MIT. The hosted services are under terms of service, not an open licence | | Failure of the accessibility floor | Pass, CLI | Inferred | A command-line tool; interactive pickers in some commands were not tested with a screen reader. The web interface was not assessed | | No exit | Pass, CLI; Unknown, hosted | Verified, Inferred | Checkpoints are ordinary git refs under `refs/entire/checkpoints/`, readable with `git for-each-ref` and kept when Entire is removed. Hosted repositories are git; the terms give at least 30 days to export after termination, except termination for material breach. Export of hosted sessions and search data is not described | ## Scorecard Ratings are for the CLI unless a row names the hosted services. | Metric area | Rating | Evidence | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | Accessibility, alternative interaction | Moderate | Inferred | Command line, with a machine-readable `entire agent-help`. Some commands open interactive pickers; non-interactive flags exist for setup. Not tested with assistive technology | | Multilingual integration | Weak | Inferred | English only, as far as the repository and site show | | Economic and cognitive accessibility | Moderate | Verified, Inferred | The CLI is free. Its model (sessions, checkpoints, refs, remotes, hooks) adds a layer to git that people must understand to keep their transcripts private. Hosted pricing is unpublished | | Representation | Unknown | None | Not assessable from public information | | Compatibility | Strong | Verified | Linux, macOS and Windows on amd64 and arm64; eight named agents; works beside existing git hook managers by chaining their hooks | | Resilience | Strong | Inferred | Checkpoints are local git objects and work offline; nothing needs the hosted service. Summaries with `--generate` call a model provider | | Agency, sovereignty and privacy | Moderate | Verified | Storing records in the repository is the right design. But pushing them by default sends full transcripts, which can quote client files, wherever the code goes, and the README itself warns that public repositories expose them. Redaction of secrets is best-effort, and PII redaction is opt-in | | Agency, power-imbalance proxies (exit cost, portability, ToS volatility, pricing asymmetry), hosted services | Weak | Verified | Entire Inc. is a Delaware company under Delaware law. The terms say Entire may modify them at any time, with continued use as acceptance. Content is licensed to Entire to operate, provide and improve the services. No general AI training without opt-in. No published pricing. No Canadian region, and the privacy policy does not mention Canada or PIPEDA | | Agency, interaction patterns | Moderate | Verified | Opt-out defaults for telemetry and session pushing. Otherwise respectful of the user's work: no commits on the active branch, `commit_linking` asks by default, and leftover shadow branches are reported rather than silently deleted | | Environment, direct, indirect, and authoring-side | Moderate | Inferred | The CLI is light. Its purpose is to keep and index every agent session, which grows repositories, and the hosted search and summaries run models. entire-graph claims up to 71% fewer agent tokens (claimed) | | Security | Moderate | Verified, Inferred | Checkpoint commits are signed by default; secrets are scanned before writing; tokens go to the OS keyring. Against that: releases carry `checksums.txt` with no signature among the assets (GitHub attestations not checked), the main install route is `curl … \| bash`, and the CLI installs git hooks and agent hooks that run on every commit and agent turn. The security policy promises acknowledgement within 48 hours. Known advisories were not checked | | Longevity | Weak | Verified, Claimed | Repository created 2026-01-02; v0.12.0, pre-1.0, with frequent changes, including a renamed Scoop package and a changed checkpoint storage format. Backed by a US$60 million seed round in February 2026 (claimed), with the risk to direction that venture funding brings | | Content endurance | Strong | Verified | Transcripts and metadata are files in git trees, in JSON and transcript formats readable without Entire | | Exit and portability | Strong, CLI; Moderate, hosted | Verified, Inferred | `entire disable --uninstall` removes hooks; checkpoint refs stay as git data or can be deleted with git. Hosted: 30 days to export after termination | | Adjustability and support | Moderate | Verified | MIT and forkable; 328 open issues and pull requests on 2026-10-21; settings per repository and per clone. Support is GitHub issues and the company | | Market position (concentration, take rate, API stability, forkability, contributor concentration) | Moderate | Verified, Claimed | 5,197 stars and 489 forks for the CLI in under ten months. A new entrant against GitHub, GitLab and Forgejo for hosting. The CLI is forkable; the hosted network is not. Contributor concentration not measured | | Gates | Pass, with conditions | Mixed | All four pass for the CLI with telemetry and session pushing configured; the hosted services' exit is Unknown | ## Findings ### Where the transcripts go Checkpoints live in the repository's own object store, each as its own ref, `refs/entire/checkpoints//`, pointing at a commit whose tree holds `metadata.json`, the transcripts and any subagent records. Nothing is written to git until a commit. The commit then carries an `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer, and the code branch never receives Entire's own commits ([Entire Inc., n.d.-d](#apa-entire-readme-reference)). `strategy_options.push_sessions` defaults to `true`, so `git push` also pushes the checkpoint refs to the same remote. For a public repository that publishes every prompt, every agent response and every quoted file. For a client repository on a forge outside Canada, it moves conversation content there as well. Redaction runs before writing, but the README calls it best-effort. Sending checkpoints to a separate private repository with `--checkpoint-remote`, or not pushing them, is the safe setting for Vishpala work. ### Fit with Universal Cake's AI transparency work The practice already marks documents as drafted with AI assistance, keeps session records (uc-automa 0016), and is assessing EU AI Act Article 50 transparency. Entire's checkpoints give a commit-level, machine-readable record of which agent, model and prompt produced which lines (`entire blame`, `entire why`), kept with the code. That is a stronger provenance record than a closing sentence, and it does not need the hosted service. It is the main reason to trial the CLI. ### Hosted services The hosted Git network, session storage and search are run by a US company under Delaware law. Regions are India, Australia, the EU and the US, with no Canadian option. The privacy policy names PostHog, Honeycomb, Datadog, HubSpot and WorkOS as subprocessors, keeps analytics and logs up to 24 months, and keeps repository content as long as the repository exists. It does not mention PIPEDA or Quebec's Law 25. Speed claims come from Entire's own benchmark, `forgemark`, and are unverified. These services do not meet the sovereignty expectations the metrics set for client data. ## Recommendation | Offering | Ring | For | |---|---|---| | Entire CLI, local checkpoints only | Assess, trial possible | A private trial on a Vishpala-owned test repository | | entire-graph | Assess | Revisit at a stable release; nightly only so far | | Hosted Git, session storage, Agentic Search | Hold, for client and Universal Cake data | Reconsider if the conditions below change | | forgemark, Rebellion | No ring | Not tools the practice would adopt | Conditions for a CLI trial: - Set `--telemetry=false` and `--skip-push-sessions` at `entire enable`, or send checkpoints to a separate private repository with `--checkpoint-remote`. - Never enable it on a repository that is or will become public, or that holds client material, until the trial has read back real transcripts and checked redaction. - Verify the release download against `checksums.txt` and install from the release archive, not through `curl | bash`. - Check that its git hooks coexist with uc-automa's pre-commit hook. The hosted services re-enter at Assess if Entire offers a Canadian region or self-hosting, publishes pricing, commits to notice before changing its terms, and documents export of sessions and search data. Re-review triggers: a 1.0 release, signed releases, a change to the default for pushing sessions, or a change to the terms or privacy policy. ## Relationship to project AI collaboration and legal or compliance. Adopted, the CLI would graduate to the AI-collaboration guidance beside `recommendation--use-a-claude-md-file`, and inform the EU AI Act transparency work in `assess/compliance/eu-ai-act/`. ## Status notes - Last reviewed: 2026-10-21 - In assess: an automated pass from public documents and repository metadata. A trial installs the CLI in a test container with the conditions above, runs a Claude Code session, and inspects the checkpoint refs, the redaction and the network contact. ## License This document, *Universal Cake Evaluation: Entire, Agent Session Capture and Git Hosting*, by **Christopher Steel**, with AI assistance from **Claude Opus 5.5 (Anthropic)**, is licensed under the [GNU Affero General Public License v3.0 or later](https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.html). ## Resources ### Evaluation framework - [Universal Cake Evaluation Metrics](#apa-uc-metrics-reference) ### Entire - [entire.io](#apa-entire-home-reference) - [Privacy policy](#apa-entire-privacy-reference) - [Terms of service](#apa-entire-terms-reference) - [Entire CLI README](#apa-entire-readme-reference) ## References Entire Inc. content.text:
I've written items 2 and 3 as drafts. I couldn't do item 1: your message arrived cut off, starting mid-word at "…h a highly accessible eleventy based website in ca-fr. ca-en and the next most widely spoken language…", so I don't know what the site is for. Nothing is committed.

## 2. Plan for osat-manager-git
`en-ca/projects/osat-manager-git/index.md`. It follows your project template and the ten stages of the OSAT manager process. Its findings come from conda-forge's own records and the recipe inside the Linux package; nothing was run.

- **Linux and macOS: conda-forge git (as you suggested).** Git 2.56.0 is built for all the main platforms. It runs on Linux systems with glibc 2.17 or later, so much older systems than dugite-native, which needs glibc 2.34.
- **Windows: MinGit, not conda-forge.** conda-forge's Windows git is just PortableGit repackaged: 121 MB, one build behind Git for Windows. The existing radar entry already recommends MinGit.
- **What conda-forge makes harder:**
  - Its packages need zstd, which Python's standard library only reads from 3.14.
  - Git needs about nine other packages, which the manager must install as a fixed, pre-resolved set.
  - The install path has to be rewritten inside 32 files, including the `git` binary itself, and those binaries then need re-signing on macOS arm64.
  - Packages carry checksums but no signatures, so the manager's own reviewed lock file becomes what we trust.
- **Five decisions are yours (D1–D5), each with a recommendation.** The main ones:
  - Require Python 3.14 or later for manage-git.
  - Build the shared manager package first (decision 0024), with conda-forge support in it, so later managers only need their own `manager.yaml`.
  - Allow one exception to the no-shell-commands rule: `codesign` on macOS.
- **Later managers.** The plan lists tools conda-forge publishes for all three platforms that could get managers the same way: git-lfs, gh, pandoc, rclone, age, typst, hugo, nodejs and ripgrep.
- **Mislabelled licence.** conda-forge labels git "GPL-2.0-or-later", but git is GPL-2.0-only. Worth reporting to them.
- **The old build sequence.** The early drafts in the `osat-manager-git/` checkout installed git through apt, dnf, Homebrew and winget. The manager rules don't allow system package managers, so the plan replaces that sequence.

`uc-automa check` reports nothing for the plan. Its remaining findings are about your existing untracked files: the two session notes have spaces in their names and no front matter, and the layout doesn't describe `en-ca/projects/`, `en-ca/policies/` or the project template.

## 3. Radar entries
Both are in uc-radar, ring Assess, against metrics 0.5.1. I wrote them from documents only; nothing was installed.

- **mise-en-place** (`assess/installers/universal-cake-evaluation--mise-en-place--polyglot-tool-version-manager-v0-1-0.md`): it passes all four gates. Its conda backend already does what manage-git would do on Linux and macOS, so it's the model to copy, not something to depend on. Main risks: only one person can change its core, and some tools still install through asdf plugins.
- **Entire** (`assess/ai-collaboration/universal-cake-evaluation--entire--agent-session-capture-and-git-hosting-v0-1-0.md`): it covers every product listed on entire.io.
  - **The CLI (MIT):** worth a private trial for tracking which AI work produced which code.
  - **Its defaults are the problem:** it pushes full session transcripts with every `git push`, and sends usage analytics to PostHog unless you turn it off.
  - **The hosted services:** I put them on Hold for client data. Entire is a Delaware company that can change its terms at any time, has no Canadian region and publishes no pricing.

I used the radar template's AGPL licence statement because uc-radar hasn't moved to CC BY 4.0 yet. Change it if you want new entries to follow decision 0025 already.

**For item 1, I need:** what the website is about, and where it should live (a new repository, or one under `sites/`). I'll take French (fr-CA), English (en-CA) and, as the third language, Spanish, Arabic or Haitian Creole, whichever is most widely spoken in Montreal per the latest census, unless you say otherwise.
