1054	title: "Self-Hosting Decision Framework — When to Run It Yourself and When Not To"
1055	navTitle: "Self-Hosting Decision Framework"
1056	order: 4
1057	identifier: "urn:uuid:7f538f3d-ea81-446c-ae61-94a99bbb5a0f"
1058	relation: "urn:uuid:2428f521-d6fb-4493-9b62-e569e02ba7ab"
1059	description: "A practical framework for deciding when self-hosting a service improves your organisation's agency and when it introduces complexity without commensurate benefit."
1060	type: "Text"
1061	---
1062	
1063	A practical framework for deciding when self-hosting a service
1064	improves your organisation's agency and when it introduces complexity
1065	without commensurate benefit.
1066	
1067	## Purpose
1068	
1069	Self-hosting is not inherently better than using a managed service.
1070	The question is always whether self-hosting, for this service, for
1071	this organisation, at this moment, produces a better outcome than the
1072	available alternatives. This framework helps structure that decision.
1073	
1074	## 1. The four questions
1075	
1076	Before deciding to self-host any service, answer four questions:
1077	
1078	1. **What do you gain?** Enumerate the specific benefits: data
1079	   sovereignty, reduced cost, elimination of a vendor dependency,
1080	   alignment with a privacy commitment, the ability to customise
1081	   behaviour the vendor will not support. Be concrete. "More control"
1082	   is not sufficient — control over what, specifically?
1083	2. **What does it cost to operate?** Self-hosted services require
1084	   someone to maintain them: applying security updates, monitoring for
1085	   failures, managing backups, and responding when things break. Who
1086	   will do this? What is their capacity? What happens when they are
1087	   unavailable?
1088	3. **What is the failure mode?** If the self-hosted service fails,
1089	   what is the impact? How quickly can it be restored? Is there a
1090	   tested recovery procedure? The failure mode of a self-hosted
1091	   service is typically your problem to solve in a way that a managed
1092	   service's failure mode is not.
1093	4. **What is the exit cost?** If self-hosting turns out to be the
1094	   wrong decision, how much effort does it take to migrate to a
1095	   managed service? Low exit cost makes the decision reversible. High
1096	   exit cost means you need to be more confident before you commit.
1097	
1098	## 2. When self-hosting is clearly the right choice
1099	
1100	Self-hosting is clearly the right choice when:
1101	
1102	- The data processed by the service is sensitive and subject to jurisdiction requirements that managed services cannot satisfy
1103	- The organisation has the operational capacity to maintain the service reliably
1104	- The managed alternatives are prohibitively expensive relative to the value delivered
1105	- The managed alternatives have unacceptable lock-in characteristics
1106	
1107	## 3. When managed services are clearly the right choice
1108	
1109	Managed services are clearly the right choice when:
1110	
1111	- The operational cost of self-hosting exceeds the cost of the managed service
1112	- The organisation does not have the capacity to respond to failures reliably
1113	- The service is not part of the organisation's core operational competence
1114	- The data processed is not sensitive and jurisdiction is not a concern
1115	
1116	## 4. The honest answer most of the time
1117	
1118	Most organisations should self-host fewer things than idealists
1119	advocate and more things than vendors prefer. The right answer depends
1120	entirely on operational capacity, data sensitivity, and the specific
1121	alternatives available. Anyone who gives you a blanket answer is not
1122	engaging with your actual situation.

1133	
1134	How vishpala.com approaches typography: system-ui as the default, with
1135	Atkinson Hyperlegible available as a user-selectable accessible
1136	alternative, self-hosted with no external dependencies.
1137	
1138	## The approach
1139	
1140	This site uses `system-ui, sans-serif` — the device's native font
1141	stack — as its default typography. No fonts are loaded from external
1142	sources. As a user-selectable alternative, Atkinson Hyperlegible is
1143	available and self-hosted: all font files are served directly from
1144	this site with no third-party requests.
1145	
1146	## System-ui — the default
1147	
1148	System fonts are the typefaces operating system vendors have spent the
1149	most resources optimising for screen legibility at every size, display
1150	density, and accessibility setting. San Francisco on macOS and iOS,
1151	Segoe UI on Windows, and Roboto on Android are each the product of
1152	significant investment in hinting, spacing, and rendering.
1153	
1154	System fonts respond correctly to the user's own font preferences. If
1155	a user has configured their operating system to use a larger default
1156	font size or a specific typeface for readability reasons, system-ui
1157	inherits those preferences. For users who depend on those preferences,
1158	that inheritance is important.
1159	
1160	`system-ui` introduces no external dependency of any kind and imposes
1161	no infrastructure maintenance burden.
1162	
1163	## Atkinson Hyperlegible — the accessible alternative
1164	
1165	Atkinson Hyperlegible was designed by the Braille Institute
1166	specifically for readers with low vision. Each character is uniquely
1167	formed to prevent misreading — the letterforms for commonly confused
1168	pairs (1/l/I, 0/O, rn/m) are deliberately differentiated. The Braille
1169	Institute released it under the SIL Open Font Licence 1.1, permitting
1170	free use and redistribution.
1171	
1172	The Inclusive Design Research Centre at OCAD University documents
1173	Atkinson Hyperlegible as a recommended typeface for low-vision
1174	accessibility.
1175	
1176	## Sovereignty and performance
1177	
1178	Neither typography option loads fonts from Google Fonts or any other
1179	external source. There is no connection to a third-party font delivery
1180	network and no disclosure of visitor IP addresses to font providers.
1181	
1182	When system-ui is active, text renders immediately using a font
1183	already present on the device — no network request, no flash of
1184	invisible text, no layout shift.

title: "Commitments"
navTitle: "Commitments"
order: 2
identifier: "urn:uuid:7c3e9a1b-4d2f-4e68-9a1c-5b8d6f2a3c4e"
relation: "urn:uuid:66666666-6666-4666-8666-666666666666"
description: "What we hold ourselves to, and why — grounded in Universal Cake, our framework for evaluating whether technology actually serves the people who use it."
type: "Text"
---

These aren't a compliance checklist. They're the practical form of
Universal Cake — our own framework for asking, before building or
choosing anything, who it actually serves and what it costs the people
who depend on it if that relationship goes wrong. Universal Cake starts
from the most fundamental requirements and builds up: a site nobody can
read can't deliver on anything else it promises.

## Accessibility

Our first commitment, because it's the one everything else depends on.
A site that's unreadable to someone using a screen reader, unusable on
an old device, or written in a language a visitor doesn't speak, has
failed before anything else about it matters. That includes people with
vision, hearing, motor, and speech differences, and it includes economic
and cognitive accessibility — whether something is affordable, learnable
without training, and forgiving of mistakes.

## Sustainability

We try not to spend other people's bandwidth, battery, or electricity by
default. Concretely, not aspirationally: every font this site uses is
served from our own servers, not fetched from a third party's — no
request to Google Fonts or any other external service just to render
text. It's a small thing on its own, and it's the kind of small thing
that adds up across millions of page loads, and across visitors on
slower or less reliable connections than the one this was built on.

## Sovereignty

You shouldn't have to trust our word that you could leave if you needed
to — you should be able to check. Every page of this site is a plain
text file, in an open format, tracked in version control. If the tools
we build with disappeared tomorrow, the content wouldn't disappear with
them.

## Data Portability

Closely tied to sovereignty, and worth naming on its own: nothing here
is locked behind a proprietary export process. What's readable by a
program is also readable by a person — a technically complete export
that only a developer can open isn't the same guarantee as one anyone
can.

## Longevity

We can't promise any particular tool we use today will still exist in
ten years — nobody honestly can. What we can commit to is choosing
plain, open formats and widely-used, forkable tools over proprietary or
fashionable ones, specifically so that the content outlives whatever
we're currently using to build it.

We are a studio of practitioners in technology, design, and
infrastructure — working with individuals and organisations who want
to operate with greater agency.

## Who we are

Vishpala is a multidisciplinary studio. We are technologists,
designers, and infrastructure specialists who work together on
problems that require all three disciplines to solve well.

We take our name from the Rigvedic figure Vishpala — a warrior who
loses a leg in battle and is given an iron prosthetic by the Ashvins
so she can return to the field. We are interested in the idea of
prosthetics: tools and infrastructure that extend capability, restore
agency, and allow people to do what they came to do.

## What we believe

**Sovereignty matters.** Organisations that depend entirely on
infrastructure they do not control are fragile in ways that are not
always visible until something breaks. We help organisations
understand their dependencies and, where it serves them, reduce them.

**Accessibility is not optional.** We do not build things that exclude
people with disabilities, and we do not help other organisations build
them. WCAG 2.2 Level AA is the floor we hold our own client work to.

**Complexity should be proportionate.** The right infrastructure for a
community organisation is not the right infrastructure for a national
one. We size solutions to the actual operational capacity of the
people who will maintain them.

**Excellence takes time.** We work on fewer things at once than most
studios. We do not take on work we cannot do well.

## How we work

We work in close collaboration with our clients throughout a project —
not in isolation with periodic check-ins. We believe the people who
will use and maintain what we build should understand it, which means
building understanding as we go rather than handing over a finished
system at the end.

We work in English and French.

Our commitment to accessibility, and the current state of this site.

## Commitment

Accessibility is the first of our [commitments](/en-ca/about/commitments/),
because everything else this site does depends on it. We treat it as a
core discipline of our practice, not a compliance exercise bolted on
at the end.

## Current measures

This site has been designed and built with accessibility as a primary
requirement. The following measures are in place:

- Semantic HTML structure with appropriate landmark regions
- A "Skip to content" link as the first focusable element on every page
- Every interactive part of the site — the language switcher, the mobile menu, all navigation links — works from a keyboard alone, with visible focus outlines on every focusable element
- The mobile menu is a native `<details>`/`<summary>` disclosure rather than a custom JavaScript widget, so it behaves the way assistive technology already expects
- Nothing on this site depends on JavaScript to be readable or navigable
- Every page declares its own language (`lang="en"` or `lang="fr"`) and alternate-language links (`hreflang`)
- Where a page has no translation yet, the language switcher shows it as missing rather than linking somewhere broken
- Meaningful images carry descriptive alt text; decorative ones don't compete for a screen reader's attention
- Diagrams are plain SVG, not flattened screenshots, so their content stays selectable and scalable
- Text resizes fluidly with the browser's own zoom and font-size settings, rather than being fixed to a pixel size
- Fonts are self-hosted (see [Commitments](/en-ca/about/commitments/)), so text still renders even when a third-party font host would otherwise block or slow the page
- Layout reflows for narrow screens and enlarged text without content being clipped or overlapping

## Known limitations

This statement describes intent and current practice, not a certified
audit or a claimed conformance level. If something on this site
doesn't work the way it's described here, that's a bug we want to
know about.

No known issues at time of publication.

## Feedback and contact

If you encounter an accessibility barrier on this site — something
that prevents you from accessing content or using a feature — tell us
what page you were on and what happened:

Email: accessibility@vishpala.com

We treat accessibility reports as a priority fix, not a backlog item.

Our commitment to privacy as a foundational principle — not a
compliance exercise. For the minimal, factual account of what this
particular site collects, see the [Privacy Policy](/en-ca/about/legal/privacy/);
this page is about the principle behind it.

## Principle

Privacy at Vishpala is not a legal obligation we satisfy at minimum
cost. It is a foundational design principle that shapes every decision
about what we build, what data we collect, and what infrastructure we
use.

We apply the seven foundational principles of Privacy by Design as
articulated by Ann Cavoukian:

- Proactive, not reactive — preventive, not remedial
- Privacy as the default setting
- Privacy embedded into design
- Full functionality — positive-sum, not zero-sum
- End-to-end security — full lifecycle protection
- Visibility and transparency
- Respect for user privacy — keep it user-centric

## What we collect and why

**This website** — we do not use analytics tracking. We do not set
cookies. We do not load third-party scripts. No data about visitors to
this site is collected, transmitted to third parties, or retained.

**Client engagements** — we collect the information necessary to
deliver our work: contact information, project materials, and
communications. We do not collect information beyond what is needed.
We do not retain client data beyond the period required for the
engagement and any applicable legal retention requirement.

**Communications** — email and other communications with us are
stored on infrastructure we operate. We do not use email marketing
platforms or CRM systems that transmit your contact information to
third parties.

## Your rights

Under the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act
(PIPEDA) and applicable provincial privacy legislation, you have the
right to:

- Know what personal information we hold about you
- Access that information
- Request correction of inaccurate information
- Withdraw consent for processing where consent is the legal basis
- Have your information deleted, subject to legal retention requirements

To exercise any of these rights, contact us at privacy@vishpala.com.

## Infrastructure

Our fonts are self-hosted — no request to Google Fonts or any other
third party just to render text. See [Commitments](/en-ca/about/commitments/)
for the rest of what that principle covers on this site.

## Contact

Questions about this policy or about how we handle personal
information: privacy@vishpala.com.

Our commitment to environmental and operational sustainability in the
work we do and how we do it.

## Principle

We build things that are meant to last. That commitment extends beyond
the technical quality of the work to its environmental and operational
footprint.

Sustainability at Vishpala means building systems that consume the
minimum necessary resources, that can be maintained by small teams
without specialised infrastructure, and that do not accumulate
complexity faster than the capacity to understand and operate them.

## Digital sustainability

**Efficient infrastructure** — we design systems sized to actual
workload. We do not recommend infrastructure at a scale that requires
constant management overhead to justify its cost or complexity.
Smaller, simpler, better-understood systems are almost always more
sustainable than large, complex ones.

**Minimal dependencies** — every dependency is a liability: a thing
that must be updated, monitored, and eventually replaced. We minimise
dependencies as a matter of practice, preferring solutions that
compose well from smaller, stable components over solutions that
introduce large dependency trees.

**Long-lived software** — we prefer technologies with long track
records and stable interfaces over technologies that require frequent
rewrites to remain current. The most sustainable software is software
that does not need to be replaced.

**No unnecessary data collection** — collecting data has an energy
cost. Storing data has an energy cost. Transmitting data has an energy
cost. We do not collect, store, or transmit data that does not serve a
clear purpose.

## Operational sustainability

**Documentation** — undocumented systems are unsustainable systems.
They accumulate technical debt invisibly and become dependent on the
continued availability of the people who built them. We treat
documentation as a core deliverable.

**Knowledge transfer** — we build with the intention that our clients
can operate, maintain, and extend what we build without us. Dependency
on an external consultant is not a sustainable operational model.

**Workload** — we do not take on more work than we can do well.
Overextended practitioners produce lower quality work and burn out. We
maintain a sustainable pace as a matter of professional principle.

## What we do not yet do

We do not currently measure or report the specific energy consumption
of the infrastructure we operate or recommend. This is a gap we intend
to address. We will update this commitment when we have a methodology
we are confident in.

type: "Text"

Conformance, remediation, and the organisational practice of building
things that work for everyone.

Accessibility is not a checklist or a compliance exercise. It is the
practice of building things that work for the full range of people who
need to use them — across abilities, devices, languages, and connection
speeds.

We approach accessibility as a discipline that runs through every stage
of a project, not a phase that happens after design and development are
complete. The cost of retrofitting accessibility is always higher than
building it in from the start.

## What we work on

**Conformance audits** — systematic evaluation of digital products
against WCAG 2.2 criteria, delivered as a prioritised remediation plan
with clear ownership and testable acceptance criteria. We audit to AA
as standard and AAA where the use case warrants it.

**Remediation** — hands-on remediation of accessibility issues in
HTML, CSS, and content, including complex cases involving dynamic
content, single-page applications, and custom interactive components.

**Procurement support** — accessibility requirements for RFPs and
vendor evaluation criteria, including evaluation of VPAT documentation
and independent testing of vendor claims.

**Organisational practice** — training, process integration, and
tooling recommendations that build accessibility competence into a
team's standard workflow rather than concentrating it in a single
specialist.

**Usability testing** — moderated testing sessions with participants
who use assistive technologies, screen readers, switch access, voice
control, and other access methods, delivering qualitative findings
that automated tools cannot surface.

## Our approach

Automated testing catches approximately 30% of accessibility issues.
The rest require human judgment. We combine automated scanning with
manual expert review and user testing because no single method is
sufficient on its own.

title: "Design"
navTitle: "Design"
order: 2
identifier: "urn:uuid:978e48fc-79fb-403e-b23b-9153b4889109"
relation: "urn:uuid:d91e8a74-a19f-474e-9eea-04b65261f43d"
description: "Accessible, multilingual design systems built to serve people — not to impress peers or satisfy platform requirements."

Accessible, multilingual design systems built to serve people — not to
impress peers or satisfy platform requirements.

We practice design as a discipline of clarity. Our work begins with the
people who will use it — their actual contexts, access levels,
languages, and needs — and builds outward from there toward visual
form, not the other way around.

Design at Vishpala is inseparable from accessibility. We treat WCAG 2.2
Level AA conformance as a floor, not a ceiling, and we test with real
people across a range of abilities and assistive technologies at every
stage of a project.

## What we work on

**Design systems** — token-based, component-level design
infrastructure that can be maintained by a small team, translated
without visual degradation, and extended without breaking existing
patterns. We build for longevity, not for the current sprint.

**Accessible interfaces** — visual design, interaction design, and
content design that work for people with a wide range of visual,
motor, cognitive, and linguistic access needs. We conduct usability
testing as a standard part of every project, not an optional extra.

**Multilingual design** — layouts and typographic systems that
function correctly in French, English, and other languages without
requiring separate design work per language. We design for the
longest string, the right-to-left edge case, and the screen reader
user simultaneously.

**Brand and visual identity** — identity systems for organisations
that need to communicate consistently across contexts without a
full-time design team. We deliver systems, not artefacts.

## Our approach

Good design is invisible to the person it serves. Our goal is never to
produce work that announces itself as design. It is to produce work
that allows the person using it to do what they came to do.

title: "Infrastructure"

order: 3

relation: "urn:uuid:d1f9cb60-df5f-4195-bdaa-5a4df3c4cab6"

---

Reproducible, auditable, sovereign systems — designed to be
understood, maintained, and owned by the people who depend on them.

We design and build infrastructure that organisations can own outright
— not in the legal sense only, but in the operational sense. Systems
they can understand, document, rebuild, and hand off without asking
permission from a vendor.

Our infrastructure practice covers the full stack from physical
hosting decisions through to deployment pipelines, monitoring, backup,
and the documentation that makes it all maintainable by a human being
at two in the morning.

## What we work on

**Deployment pipelines** — reproducible build and deployment systems
that treat infrastructure as code, version-controlled and auditable.
We prefer simple, composable tools over platforms that abstract away
operational understanding.

**Self-hosted services** — migration away from proprietary SaaS
platforms toward open, self-operated alternatives where this serves
the organisation's sovereignty and privacy commitments. We do not
advocate self-hosting for its own sake; we advocate it where it
materially improves an organisation's agency.

**Operational documentation** — runbooks, architecture diagrams, and
recovery procedures that reflect the actual system, not an idealised
version of it. Documentation is treated as a first-class deliverable,
not an afterthought.

**Resilience and recovery** — backup systems with tested restore
procedures, incident response planning, and the kind of redundancy
that matches the actual risk profile of the organisation rather than
the risk profile of a much larger one.

## Our approach

We work from first principles rather than from a preferred tool stack.
The right infrastructure for a community health clinic is not the
right infrastructure for a national media organisation. We size the
complexity of the solution to the operational capacity of the team
that will maintain it.

A complete design system and component library for a national NGO
operating in four languages — built for accessibility from the ground
up, maintainable by a small internal team, and independent of any
proprietary design toolchain.

## Overview

A national non-governmental organisation with programmes across twelve
provinces needed a coherent visual identity and digital presence that
could be maintained by a team of three non-specialist staff, translated
into four languages without design degradation, and used confidently
by people with a wide range of disabilities and technical access
levels.

The brief was explicit on two points: the system had to work without a
subscription to any design tool, and it had to achieve WCAG 2.2 Level
AA conformance at every touchpoint.

## Approach

We audited the existing digital presence and identified the thirty
most frequently used interface patterns. From these we derived a
minimal design token system: twelve colours, four type sizes, three
spacing scales. Everything else is composed from these primitives.

The component library was built in plain HTML and CSS — no framework
dependency, no build step for basic use. Each component ships with its
accessibility annotations, keyboard interaction model, and a
plain-language description suitable for non-technical staff.
Translations are managed through a simple key-value file per language,
requiring no design changes to switch languages.

We ran usability testing with twelve participants across three
disability categories and three levels of digital literacy before
finalising the system.

## Outcome

The NGO's digital presence is now consistent across all twelve
provincial sites. The internal team has shipped four major content
updates and one new programme page without external support. Automated
accessibility testing passes at 100% on all core pages. The French,
Cree, Inuktitut, and English versions are maintained in parallel by a
single content coordinator.

## What we built

- Design token system (colour, type, spacing)
- 30-component HTML/CSS library with full accessibility annotations
- Translation infrastructure (key-value i18n, no framework required)
- WCAG 2.2 Level AA conformance audit and remediation
- Staff training materials and maintenance guide
- Ongoing quarterly accessibility review process

A full infrastructure pivot away from proprietary cloud lock-in for a
regional health network serving 80,000 patients — replacing
vendor-managed services with reproducible, self-hosted, auditable
systems under the organisation's own operational control.

## Overview

A regional health network operating across six sites had accumulated
deep dependencies on three separate proprietary cloud platforms over
eight years of growth. The infrastructure was functional but opaque:
no single person understood the full system, vendor contracts were
auto-renewing without review, and patient data was processed across
jurisdictions in ways that were inconsistent with the organisation's
own privacy commitments.

We were brought in to design and implement a path to operational
independence — one that did not require a "big bang" cutover and did
not introduce new categories of fragility in the process of removing
old ones.

## Approach

We began with a full infrastructure audit: every service, every data
flow, every external dependency mapped and documented. From that
baseline we identified three categories of dependency — those that
could be eliminated immediately, those requiring phased migration, and
those where a sovereign alternative did not yet exist and would need
to be built.

The migration ran over fourteen months across four phases. We
prioritised patient data first, moving all clinical records to a
self-hosted, jurisdiction-compliant system with automated backup
verification and a tested restore procedure. We replaced the
vendor-managed identity system with an open, auditable alternative. We
decommissioned two SaaS platforms entirely by consolidating their
functions into tools the organisation already operated.

## Outcome

The network now operates a fully documented, reproducible
infrastructure. Every service can be rebuilt from version-controlled
configuration. The on-call team can understand the full system in a
single working day. Annual vendor contract costs were reduced by 68%.
The organisation's privacy commitments and its actual infrastructure
are now consistent with each other.

## What we built

- Full infrastructure audit and dependency map
- Phased migration plan with rollback procedures at each stage
- Self-hosted clinical records system with automated backup and restore testing
- Open identity and access management platform
- Runbooks and operational documentation for the internal team
- Training programme for three tiers of operational staff

type: "Text"

A checklist for evaluating accessibility claims during software
procurement — covering VPAT review, independent testing, contractual
commitments, and what to do when a vendor cannot answer your
questions.

## Purpose

Most software vendors will tell you their product is accessible. This
checklist helps you evaluate that claim before you sign a contract,
not after you have committed to a platform your users cannot use.

## 1. Ask for the VPAT

A Voluntary Product Accessibility Template (VPAT) is a vendor's
self-reported assessment of how their product conforms to
accessibility standards. Ask for the VPAT for the specific version of
the product you are evaluating, against WCAG 2.2 Level AA.

Red flags in a VPAT:

- It references WCAG 2.0 or 2.1 rather than 2.2
- Every criterion is listed as "Supports" with no explanation
- The evaluation was conducted by the vendor itself with no independent review
- It covers a version of the product that is more than one major release old

## 2. Test independently

Do not rely on the VPAT alone. Conduct or commission independent
testing before purchase. At minimum:

- Run an automated scan using a current tool (Axe, WAVE, or equivalent)
- Navigate the core user flows using only a keyboard
- Test with a screen reader (NVDA on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS and iOS)
- Check colour contrast on all text and interactive elements

## 3. Ask contractual questions

Before signing, ask:

- What is the vendor's published accessibility conformance target?
- What is the process for reporting accessibility issues?
- What is the committed remediation timeframe for critical accessibility barriers?
- Are accessibility commitments included in the SLA?

A vendor who cannot answer these questions is a vendor who has not
made accessibility a priority. That is useful information.

## 4. When a vendor cannot meet your requirements

If a vendor cannot demonstrate conformance and will not make
contractual commitments, you have three options: require conformance
as a condition of contract, require a remediation plan with milestones
as a condition of contract, or choose a different vendor.

Accepting an inaccessible product because it meets other requirements
is a decision that excludes some of your users. That decision should
be made explicitly and documented, not absorbed quietly into a
procurement process.

---

A plain-language introduction to design tokens: what they are, why
they matter for multilingual and accessible design, and how to
implement a minimal token system without a design tool subscription.

## What is a design token?

A design token is a named value that encodes a design decision.
Instead of writing `color: #0033cc` in five hundred places, you define
a token — `--colour-primary: #0033cc` — and reference the token
everywhere. When the decision changes, you change it in one place.

Tokens are the infrastructure layer of a design system. They are not a
design tool feature or a framework requirement. They are CSS custom
properties, and they work in any browser.

## Why tokens matter for accessible, multilingual design

**Accessibility** — tokens make it tractable to verify colour contrast
across an entire system. If your text colour and background colour are
both tokens, you can check every combination in one place rather than
hunting through a codebase for hardcoded values.

**Multilingual design** — tokens make it straightforward to adjust
typographic decisions for specific languages. A French interface may
need slightly more generous line height than an English one. A
token-based system lets you override a single value per language
rather than rewriting layout rules.

**Maintainability** — a small team can maintain a token-based system
because changes are localised. Replacing the primary colour takes two
minutes, not two days.

## A minimal token system

A minimal token system for a small organisation typically needs four
categories:

- **Colour** — three to five colours maximum. A primary colour, a text colour, a background colour, a border colour, and one semantic colour (for errors or warnings if needed). Every other colour in the system should be derived from these or be black or white.
- **Typography** — two to three font sizes for body text, one or two for headings, and one for small labels. A line height for each. A font stack per typeface used.
- **Spacing** — four to six spacing values on a consistent scale, e.g. 0.25rem, 0.5rem, 1rem, 2rem, 4rem. Everything else is composed from these.
- **Layout** — a maximum content width and a standard gap value for grid layouts.

## Implementation

```css
:root {
  --colour-primary: #0033cc;
  --colour-text: #000000;
  --colour-background: #ffffff;
  --colour-border: #d0d0d0;
  --font-body: system-ui, sans-serif;
  --size-sm: 0.875rem;
  --size-base: 1rem;
  --size-lg: 1.25rem;
  --size-xl: 1.75rem;
  --space-sm: 0.5rem;
  --space-md: 1rem;
  --space-lg: 2rem;
  --space-xl: 4rem;
  --measure: 70ch;
}
```

That's a complete minimal token system. Everything else is
composition.

title: "Infrastructure Audit Guide — Mapping What You Have Before Changing It"
navTitle: "Infrastructure Audit Guide"
order: 2
identifier: "urn:uuid:2c87d848-fc95-4690-934f-379292d5f582"
relation: "urn:uuid:b11022df-d208-4fb2-9f19-27e4677cab01"
description: "A practical guide to conducting a full infrastructure audit: what to document, how to surface hidden dependencies, and how to produce a map that is actually useful for decision-making."
type: "Text"
---

A practical guide to conducting a full infrastructure audit: what to
document, how to surface hidden dependencies, and how to produce a map
that is actually useful for decision-making.

## Purpose

Before any infrastructure work begins, you need an accurate picture of
what exists. This guide describes how to conduct a full infrastructure
audit — not a theoretical inventory, but a working document that
reflects the system as it actually operates.

## 1. What to capture

A useful infrastructure audit captures six categories of information:

- **Services** — every running service, its purpose, its operator, and its dependencies
- **Data flows** — where data originates, where it is processed, where it is stored, and where it leaves your control
- **Access and credentials** — who has access to what, under what authentication model, and where credentials are stored
- **External dependencies** — every third-party service, API, or platform the system depends on
- **Contracts and costs** — every vendor contract, its renewal date, its cost, and what it would take to exit it
- **Documentation** — what documentation exists, how current it is, and where it lives

## 2. How to surface hidden dependencies

Hidden dependencies are the most dangerous part of any infrastructure.
They are things the system depends on that nobody has explicitly
decided to depend on — accumulated through years of pragmatic
decisions that were never revisited.

Common sources of hidden dependencies include:

- DNS records pointing to services that no longer exist but whose removal would break something
- Email delivery relying on a personal account held by a former employee
- Authentication flows that pass through a third-party service inserted years ago as a temporary measure
- Backup jobs that write to a location that has quietly run out of space
- SSL certificates managed by a person who has left the organisation

The most reliable way to surface hidden dependencies is to map data
flows from the outside in: start from every public-facing URL and
follow each request through the system until it reaches persistent
storage or exits to a third party.

## 3. Producing a useful map

An infrastructure map is only useful if it reflects the actual system
and can be read by someone who did not build it. It should include:

- A diagram showing major components and the connections between them
- A table of services with owner, dependencies, and last-verified date
- A list of external dependencies with contract and cost information
- A list of open questions that the audit surfaced but could not resolve

The map should be version-controlled alongside the infrastructure it
describes and updated whenever a significant change is made.

title: "Self-Hosting Decision Framework — When to Run It Yourself and When Not To"
navTitle: "Self-Hosting Decision Framework"
order: 4
identifier: "urn:uuid:7f538f3d-ea81-446c-ae61-94a99bbb5a0f"
relation: "urn:uuid:2428f521-d6fb-4493-9b62-e569e02ba7ab"
description: "A practical framework for deciding when self-hosting a service improves your organisation's agency and when it introduces complexity without commensurate benefit."
type: "Text"
---

A practical framework for deciding when self-hosting a service
improves your organisation's agency and when it introduces complexity
without commensurate benefit.

## Purpose

Self-hosting is not inherently better than using a managed service.
The question is always whether self-hosting, for this service, for
this organisation, at this moment, produces a better outcome than the
available alternatives. This framework helps structure that decision.

## 1. The four questions

Before deciding to self-host any service, answer four questions:

1. **What do you gain?** Enumerate the specific benefits: data
   sovereignty, reduced cost, elimination of a vendor dependency,
   alignment with a privacy commitment, the ability to customise
   behaviour the vendor will not support. Be concrete. "More control"
   is not sufficient — control over what, specifically?
2. **What does it cost to operate?** Self-hosted services require
   someone to maintain them: applying security updates, monitoring for
   failures, managing backups, and responding when things break. Who
   will do this? What is their capacity? What happens when they are
   unavailable?
3. **What is the failure mode?** If the self-hosted service fails,
   what is the impact? How quickly can it be restored? Is there a
   tested recovery procedure? The failure mode of a self-hosted
   service is typically your problem to solve in a way that a managed
   service's failure mode is not.
4. **What is the exit cost?** If self-hosting turns out to be the
   wrong decision, how much effort does it take to migrate to a
   managed service? Low exit cost makes the decision reversible. High
   exit cost means you need to be more confident before you commit.

## 2. When self-hosting is clearly the right choice

Self-hosting is clearly the right choice when:

- The data processed by the service is sensitive and subject to jurisdiction requirements that managed services cannot satisfy
- The organisation has the operational capacity to maintain the service reliably
- The managed alternatives are prohibitively expensive relative to the value delivered
- The managed alternatives have unacceptable lock-in characteristics

## 3. When managed services are clearly the right choice

Managed services are clearly the right choice when:

- The operational cost of self-hosting exceeds the cost of the managed service
- The organisation does not have the capacity to respond to failures reliably
- The service is not part of the organisation's core operational competence
- The data processed is not sensitive and jurisdiction is not a concern

## 4. The honest answer most of the time

Most organisations should self-host fewer things than idealists
advocate and more things than vendors prefer. The right answer depends
entirely on operational capacity, data sensitivity, and the specific
alternatives available. Anyone who gives you a blanket answer is not
engaging with your actual situation.

---

How vishpala.com approaches typography: system-ui as the default, with
Atkinson Hyperlegible available as a user-selectable accessible
alternative, self-hosted with no external dependencies.

## The approach

This site uses `system-ui, sans-serif` — the device's native font
stack — as its default typography. No fonts are loaded from external
sources. As a user-selectable alternative, Atkinson Hyperlegible is
available and self-hosted: all font files are served directly from
this site with no third-party requests.

## System-ui — the default

System fonts are the typefaces operating system vendors have spent the
most resources optimising for screen legibility at every size, display
density, and accessibility setting. San Francisco on macOS and iOS,
Segoe UI on Windows, and Roboto on Android are each the product of
significant investment in hinting, spacing, and rendering.

System fonts respond correctly to the user's own font preferences. If
a user has configured their operating system to use a larger default
font size or a specific typeface for readability reasons, system-ui
inherits those preferences. For users who depend on those preferences,
that inheritance is important.

`system-ui` introduces no external dependency of any kind and imposes
no infrastructure maintenance burden.

## Atkinson Hyperlegible — the accessible alternative

Atkinson Hyperlegible was designed by the Braille Institute
specifically for readers with low vision. Each character is uniquely
formed to prevent misreading — the letterforms for commonly confused
pairs (1/l/I, 0/O, rn/m) are deliberately differentiated. The Braille
Institute released it under the SIL Open Font Licence 1.1, permitting
free use and redistribution.

The Inclusive Design Research Centre at OCAD University documents
Atkinson Hyperlegible as a recommended typeface for low-vision
accessibility.

## Sovereignty and performance

Neither typography option loads fonts from Google Fonts or any other
external source. There is no connection to a third-party font delivery
network and no disclosure of visitor IP addresses to font providers.

When system-ui is active, text renders immediately using a font
already present on the device — no network request, no flash of
invisible text, no layout shift.

# Sveltia CMS config (Decap-compatible format).
#
# backend.name is github, matching this repo — NOT a placeholder to
# swap later. Sveltia CMS dropped Git Gateway support entirely (not
# just discouraged — genuinely unimplemented, confirmed directly
# against Sveltia's own docs: "Bitbucket, Gitea/Forgejo and Git Gateway
# backends will not be supported due to performance limitations"), so
# `git-gateway` here wasn't a deferred config choice, it was a config
# that could never have worked. Supported backends as of writing:
# github, gitlab, gitea (self-hosted Gitea/Forgejo), test (an in-memory
# backend for trying the CMS without touching real files).
#
# For LOCAL testing without setting up GitHub OAuth: Sveltia's Local
# Development Workflow lets you skip auth entirely — run the dev
# server, open /admin/index.html in Chrome or Edge, and click "Work
# with Local Repository" to grant File System Access API permission on
# this project's root folder directly. No proxy server, no OAuth app,
# no local_backend config flag needed (that's the old Decap mechanism;
# Sveltia replaced it with this). Real remote access (from anywhere,
# not just this machine) does need OAuth — either Sveltia's own
# Authenticator (deployable to Cloudflare Workers) or a personal access
# token; not configured here, since it's not needed for local
# verification of the fixes in this file.
backend:
  name: github
  repo: steelcj/vishpala-eleventy-mvp
  branch: main

site_url: https://vishpala.com
logo_url: /assets/img/logos/logo-lockup-dark.svg

# Per-entry relative media: with an empty collection-level media_folder,
# Sveltia/Decap resolve a field's relative media_folder against the entry
# being edited, so an image field with media_folder: "index.assets" lands
# beside that entry's own index.md. Verify this against Sveltia's current
# docs before relying on it in production — media-folder resolution rules
# have shifted between CMS versions.
media_folder: ""
public_folder: ""

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------
# File Collections model (migrated from Folder Collections).
#
# WHY: Sveltia CMS cannot create new nested folders through its UI —
# confirmed directly from the maintainer (github.com/sveltia/sveltia-cms
# discussions #598): "a non-dev user wouldn't be able to create a new
# folder in the sidebar... one of our unimplemented features... it will
# be added to Sveltia CMS 2.0." The old Folder Collections
# (path: "{{slug}}/index") could never reach two-level-deep pages like

# Sveltia CMS config (Decap-compatible format).
#
# backend.name is github, matching this repo — NOT a placeholder to
# swap later. Sveltia CMS dropped Git Gateway support entirely (not
# just discouraged — genuinely unimplemented, confirmed directly
# against Sveltia's own docs: "Bitbucket, Gitea/Forgejo and Git Gateway
# backends will not be supported due to performance limitations"), so
# `git-gateway` here wasn't a deferred config choice, it was a config
# that could never have worked. Supported backends as of writing:
# github, gitlab, gitea (self-hosted Gitea/Forgejo), test (an in-memory
# backend for trying the CMS without touching real files).
#
# For LOCAL testing without setting up GitHub OAuth: Sveltia's Local
# Development Workflow lets you skip auth entirely — run the dev
# server, open /admin/index.html in Chrome or Edge, and click "Work
# with Local Repository" to grant File System Access API permission on
# this project's root folder directly. No proxy server, no OAuth app,
# no local_backend config flag needed (that's the old Decap mechanism;
# Sveltia replaced it with this). Real remote access (from anywhere,
# not just this machine) does need OAuth — either Sveltia's own

"""Write the es-ca Expressions of every Work that exists in both en-ca and fr-ca.

Run with the site root as the only argument. Each page gets a fresh
urn:uuid identifier (random, version 4, as `uuidgen -r` makes) and the
same relation UUID as its en-ca and fr-ca counterparts. Refuses to
overwrite an existing file.
"""
import json
import sys
import uuid
from pathlib import Path

ROOT = Path(sys.argv[1]) / "content" / "es-ca"


def q(value):
    return json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False)


def page(path, fm, body):
    target = ROOT / path
    if target.exists():
        raise SystemExit(f"refusing to overwrite {target}")
    lines = ["---"]
    for key in ("title", "navTitle", "order"):
        if key in fm:
            v = fm[key]
            lines.append(f"{key}: {v if isinstance(v, int) else q(v)}")
    lines.append(f'identifier: "urn:uuid:{uuid.uuid4()}"')
    lines.append(f'relation: "{fm["relation"]}"')
    for key in ("layout", "description", "coverage"):
        if key in fm:
            lines.append(f"{key}: {q(fm[key])}")
    lines.append('type: "Text"')
    for key in ("headerMenu", "footerMenu"):
        if key in fm:
            lines.append(f"{key}: {'true' if fm[key] else 'false'}")
    lines.append("---")
    text = "\n".join(lines) + "\n" + ("\n" + body.strip() + "\n" if body.strip() else "")
    target.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    target.write_text(text, encoding="utf-8")
    print(target.relative_to(ROOT.parent.parent))


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- Home
page("index.md", {
    "title": "Inicio", "navTitle": "Inicio", "order": 0,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111",
    "layout": "layouts/home.njk",
    "description": "Vishpala, un estudio de profesionales en tecnología, diseño e infraestructura.",

page("proyectos/sovereign-stack.md", {
    "title": "Sovereign Stack — Independencia de infraestructura para una red regional de salud",
    "navTitle": "Sovereign Stack", "order": 1,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:f7670414-604a-4185-9121-f85e26f4f46f",
    "description": "Un cambio completo de infraestructura para salir de la dependencia de nubes propietarias en una red regional de salud que atiende a 80 000 pacientes, reemplazando servicios gestionados por proveedores con sistemas reproducibles, autoalojados y auditables bajo el control operativo de la propia organización.",
    "coverage": "Marzo de 2026, completado",
}, """
Un cambio completo de infraestructura para salir de la dependencia de
nubes propietarias en una red regional de salud que atiende a 80 000
pacientes, reemplazando servicios gestionados por proveedores con
sistemas reproducibles, autoalojados y auditables bajo el control
operativo de la propia organización.

## Panorama general

Una red regional de salud que opera en seis sedes había acumulado, en
ocho años de crecimiento, dependencias profundas de tres plataformas de
nube propietarias distintas. La infraestructura funcionaba, pero era
opaca: nadie entendía el sistema completo, los contratos con
proveedores se renovaban automáticamente sin revisión y los datos de
pacientes se procesaban en distintas jurisdicciones de maneras
incompatibles con los compromisos de privacidad de la propia
organización.

Nos llamaron para diseñar y poner en marcha un camino hacia la
independencia operativa: uno que no exigiera un cambio de golpe y que
no introdujera nuevas formas de fragilidad mientras se eliminaban las
antiguas.

## Enfoque

Empezamos con una auditoría completa de la infraestructura: cada
servicio, cada flujo de datos y cada dependencia externa, mapeados y
documentados. A partir de esa base identificamos tres categorías de
dependencias: las que se podían eliminar de inmediato, las que
requerían una migración por fases y aquellas para las que todavía no
existía una alternativa soberana y habría que construirla.

La migración duró catorce meses, en cuatro fases. Dimos prioridad a los
datos de pacientes: trasladamos todos los expedientes clínicos a un
sistema autoalojado y conforme a la jurisdicción, con verificación
automática de las copias de seguridad y un procedimiento de
restauración probado. Reemplazamos el sistema de identidad gestionado
por el proveedor con una alternativa abierta y auditable. Dimos de baja
por completo dos plataformas SaaS, consolidando sus funciones en
herramientas que la organización ya operaba.

## Resultado

Hoy la red opera una infraestructura totalmente documentada y
reproducible. Cada servicio se puede reconstruir a partir de una
configuración bajo control de versiones. El equipo de guardia puede
entender el sistema completo en una sola jornada de trabajo. El costo
anual de los contratos con proveedores se redujo un 68 %. Los
compromisos de privacidad de la organización y su infraestructura real
ahora son coherentes entre sí.

## Lo que construimos

- Auditoría completa de la infraestructura y mapa de dependencias
- Plan de migración por fases, con procedimientos de reversión en cada etapa
- Sistema autoalojado de expedientes clínicos, con copias de seguridad automáticas y pruebas de restauración
- Plataforma abierta de gestión de identidades y accesos
- Manuales de operación y documentación operativa para el equipo interno
- Programa de formación para tres niveles de personal operativo
""")

page("proyectos/agency-design-system.md", {
    "title": "Agency Design System — Infraestructura de diseño accesible y multilingüe para una ONG nacional",
    "navTitle": "Agency Design System", "order": 2,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:54debb25-b7b3-46e8-9bae-32cca1674d64",
    "description": "Un sistema de diseño y una biblioteca de componentes completos para una ONG nacional que trabaja en cuatro idiomas: accesible desde la base, mantenible por un pequeño equipo interno e independiente de cualquier herramienta de diseño propietaria.",
    "coverage": "Enero de 2026, completado",
}, """
Un sistema de diseño y una biblioteca de componentes completos para una
ONG nacional que trabaja en cuatro idiomas: accesible desde la base,
mantenible por un pequeño equipo interno e independiente de cualquier
herramienta de diseño propietaria.

## Panorama general

Una organización no gubernamental nacional, con programas en doce
provincias, necesitaba una identidad visual y una presencia digital
coherentes que pudiera mantener un equipo de tres personas no
especialistas, que pudieran traducirse a cuatro idiomas sin degradar el
diseño y que pudieran usar con confianza personas con una gran
diversidad de discapacidades y niveles de acceso a la tecnología.

El encargo era explícito en dos puntos: el sistema tenía que funcionar
sin suscripción a ninguna herramienta de diseño y tenía que cumplir el
nivel AA de las WCAG 2.2 en todos los puntos de contacto.

## Enfoque

Auditamos la presencia digital existente e identificamos los treinta
patrones de interfaz más usados. A partir de ellos definimos un sistema
mínimo de tokens de diseño: doce colores, cuatro tamaños de letra y
tres escalas de espaciado. Todo lo demás se compone a partir de estos
elementos básicos.

La biblioteca de componentes se construyó en HTML y CSS sencillos: sin
dependencia de ningún framework y sin paso de compilación para el uso
básico. Cada componente incluye sus anotaciones de accesibilidad, su
modelo de interacción con teclado y una descripción en lenguaje claro
pensada para personal no técnico. Las traducciones se gestionan con un
archivo sencillo de claves y valores por idioma, de modo que cambiar de
idioma no requiere ningún cambio de diseño.

Antes de cerrar el sistema hicimos pruebas de usabilidad con doce
participantes de tres categorías de discapacidad y tres niveles de
alfabetización digital.

## Resultado

La presencia digital de la ONG ahora es coherente en los doce sitios
provinciales. El equipo interno ha publicado cuatro actualizaciones
importantes de contenido y una nueva página de programa sin apoyo
externo. Las pruebas automáticas de accesibilidad pasan al 100 % en
todas las páginas principales. Las versiones en francés, cree,
inuktitut e inglés las mantiene en paralelo una sola persona
coordinadora de contenido.

## Lo que construimos

- Sistema de tokens de diseño (color, tipografía, espaciado)
- Biblioteca HTML/CSS de 30 componentes con anotaciones de accesibilidad completas
- Infraestructura de traducción (i18n con claves y valores, sin framework)
- Auditoría de conformidad con las WCAG 2.2 nivel AA y corrección de problemas
- Materiales de formación para el personal y guía de mantenimiento
- Proceso trimestral continuo de revisión de accesibilidad
""")

page("areas/accesibilidad.md", {
    "title": "Accesibilidad", "navTitle": "Accesibilidad", "order": 1,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:aefeb911-7926-410b-bfb8-d466a7bc0033",
    "description": "Conformidad, corrección y la práctica organizacional de construir cosas que funcionen para todas las personas.",
}, """
Conformidad, corrección y la práctica organizacional de construir cosas
que funcionen para todas las personas.

La accesibilidad no es una lista de verificación ni un trámite de
cumplimiento. Es la práctica de construir cosas que funcionen para
toda la gama de personas que necesitan usarlas, con distintas
capacidades, dispositivos, idiomas y velocidades de conexión.

Abordamos la accesibilidad como una disciplina presente en cada etapa
de un proyecto, no como una fase que llega después del diseño y el
desarrollo. Adaptar la accesibilidad al final siempre cuesta más que
incorporarla desde el principio.

## En qué trabajamos

**Auditorías de conformidad**: evaluación sistemática de productos
digitales según los criterios de las WCAG 2.2, entregada como un plan
de corrección priorizado, con responsables claros y criterios de
aceptación verificables. Auditamos al nivel AA de forma estándar y al
nivel AAA cuando el caso de uso lo justifica.

**Corrección**: corrección práctica de problemas de accesibilidad en
HTML, CSS y contenido, incluidos casos complejos con contenido
dinámico, aplicaciones de una sola página y componentes interactivos a
medida.

**Apoyo en adquisiciones**: requisitos de accesibilidad para
licitaciones y criterios de evaluación de proveedores, incluida la
revisión de la documentación VPAT y pruebas independientes de lo que
afirman los proveedores.

**Práctica organizacional**: formación, integración en los procesos y
recomendaciones de herramientas que incorporan la competencia en
accesibilidad al flujo de trabajo habitual de un equipo, en lugar de
concentrarla en una sola persona especialista.

**Pruebas de usabilidad**: sesiones moderadas con participantes que
usan tecnologías de apoyo, lectores de pantalla, acceso por
conmutador, control por voz y otros métodos de acceso, con hallazgos
cualitativos que las herramientas automáticas no pueden detectar.

## Nuestro enfoque

Las pruebas automáticas detectan alrededor del 30 % de los problemas de
accesibilidad. El resto requiere criterio humano. Combinamos el
análisis automático con la revisión manual experta y las pruebas con
usuarios, porque ningún método es suficiente por sí solo.
""")

page("areas/diseno.md", {
    "title": "Diseño", "navTitle": "Diseño", "order": 2,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:d91e8a74-a19f-474e-9eea-04b65261f43d",
    "description": "Sistemas de diseño accesibles y multilingües, hechos para servir a las personas y no para impresionar a colegas ni para cumplir los requisitos de una plataforma.",
}, """
Sistemas de diseño accesibles y multilingües, hechos para servir a las
personas y no para impresionar a colegas ni para cumplir los
requisitos de una plataforma.

Practicamos el diseño como una disciplina de la claridad. Nuestro
trabajo empieza por las personas que lo van a usar, con sus contextos
reales, niveles de acceso, idiomas y necesidades, y desde ahí avanza
hacia la forma visual, no al revés.

En Vishpala, el diseño es inseparable de la accesibilidad. Tratamos el
nivel AA de las WCAG 2.2 como un mínimo y no como un techo, y hacemos
pruebas con personas reales, con distintas capacidades y tecnologías de
apoyo, en cada etapa de un proyecto.

## En qué trabajamos

**Sistemas de diseño**: infraestructura de diseño basada en tokens y
componentes, que un equipo pequeño puede mantener, traducir sin
degradación visual y ampliar sin romper los patrones existentes.
Construimos para que dure, no para el sprint actual.

**Interfaces accesibles**: diseño visual, de interacción y de contenido
que funciona para personas con una amplia gama de necesidades de
acceso visuales, motoras, cognitivas y lingüísticas. Las pruebas de
usabilidad son parte habitual de cada proyecto, no un extra opcional.

**Diseño multilingüe**: maquetaciones y sistemas tipográficos que
funcionan correctamente en francés, inglés, español y otros idiomas
sin requerir un diseño aparte para cada idioma. Diseñamos a la vez
para la cadena de texto más larga, para el caso de escritura de
derecha a izquierda y para la persona que usa un lector de pantalla.

**Marca e identidad visual**: sistemas de identidad para
organizaciones que necesitan comunicar de forma coherente en distintos
contextos sin un equipo de diseño a tiempo completo. Entregamos
sistemas, no piezas sueltas.

## Nuestro enfoque

El buen diseño pasa desapercibido para la persona a la que sirve.
Nuestro objetivo nunca es producir un trabajo que se anuncie como
diseño, sino uno que permita a quien lo usa hacer lo que vino a hacer.
""")

page("areas/infraestructura.md", {
    "title": "Infraestructura", "navTitle": "Infraestructura", "order": 3,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:d1f9cb60-df5f-4195-bdaa-5a4df3c4cab6",
    "description": "Sistemas reproducibles, auditables y soberanos, diseñados para que las personas que dependen de ellos puedan entenderlos, mantenerlos y ser sus dueñas.",
}, """
Sistemas reproducibles, auditables y soberanos, diseñados para que las
personas que dependen de ellos puedan entenderlos, mantenerlos y ser
sus dueñas.

Diseñamos y construimos infraestructura que las organizaciones pueden
poseer por completo, no solo en el sentido legal sino también en el
operativo: sistemas que pueden entender, documentar, reconstruir y
traspasar sin pedirle permiso a un proveedor.

Nuestra práctica de infraestructura abarca todo el conjunto, desde las
decisiones de alojamiento físico hasta los flujos de despliegue, la
supervisión, las copias de seguridad y la documentación que hace que
todo pueda mantenerlo un ser humano a las dos de la mañana.

## En qué trabajamos

**Flujos de despliegue**: sistemas de compilación y despliegue
reproducibles que tratan la infraestructura como código, bajo control
de versiones y auditable. Preferimos herramientas sencillas y
combinables a plataformas que ocultan la comprensión operativa.

**Servicios autoalojados**: migración desde plataformas SaaS
propietarias hacia alternativas abiertas y operadas por la propia
organización, cuando esto sirve a sus compromisos de soberanía y
privacidad. No defendemos el autoalojamiento por sí mismo; lo
defendemos cuando mejora de manera concreta la capacidad de acción de
una organización.

**Documentación operativa**: manuales de operación, diagramas de
arquitectura y procedimientos de recuperación que reflejan el sistema
real, no una versión idealizada. La documentación es un entregable de
primer nivel, no algo que se deja para después.

**Resiliencia y recuperación**: sistemas de copias de seguridad con
procedimientos de restauración probados, planes de respuesta a
incidentes y el tipo de redundancia que corresponde al perfil de riesgo
real de la organización, y no al de una mucho más grande.

## Nuestro enfoque

Trabajamos a partir de principios básicos y no de un conjunto de
herramientas preferido. La infraestructura adecuada para una clínica
de salud comunitaria no es la adecuada para un medio de comunicación
nacional. Ajustamos la complejidad de la solución a la capacidad
operativa del equipo que la va a mantener.
""")

page("recursos/tipografia.md", {
    "title": "Tipografía — Fuentes del sistema y Atkinson Hyperlegible",
    "navTitle": "Tipografía", "order": 1,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:1e3272f9-16d7-4585-bd20-01e3c011176a",
    "description": "Cómo aborda vishpala.com la tipografía: system-ui como opción predeterminada y Atkinson Hyperlegible como alternativa accesible que cada persona puede elegir, alojada en nuestros propios servidores y sin dependencias externas.",
}, """
Cómo aborda vishpala.com la tipografía: system-ui como opción
predeterminada y Atkinson Hyperlegible como alternativa accesible que
cada persona puede elegir, alojada en nuestros propios servidores y
sin dependencias externas.

## El enfoque

Este sitio usa `system-ui, sans-serif`, es decir, las fuentes nativas
del dispositivo, como tipografía predeterminada. No se carga ninguna
fuente desde fuentes externas. Como alternativa que cada persona puede
elegir, Atkinson Hyperlegible está disponible y alojada aquí mismo:
todos los archivos de fuentes se sirven directamente desde este sitio,
sin solicitudes a terceros.

## System-ui, la opción predeterminada

Las fuentes del sistema son los tipos de letra en los que los
fabricantes de sistemas operativos más han invertido para que se lean
bien en pantalla en cualquier tamaño, densidad de pantalla y ajuste de
accesibilidad. San Francisco en macOS e iOS, Segoe UI en Windows y
Roboto en Android son el resultado de una inversión considerable en
hinting, espaciado y renderizado.

Las fuentes del sistema respetan las preferencias de cada persona. Si
alguien configuró su sistema operativo con un tamaño de letra mayor o
con un tipo de letra específico para leer mejor, system-ui hereda esas
preferencias. Para quienes dependen de ellas, esa herencia es
importante.

`system-ui` no introduce ninguna dependencia externa ni impone ninguna
carga de mantenimiento de infraestructura.

## Atkinson Hyperlegible, la alternativa accesible

Atkinson Hyperlegible fue diseñada por el Braille Institute
específicamente para lectores con baja visión. Cada carácter tiene una
forma única para evitar confusiones: las letras de los pares que más
se confunden (1/l/I, 0/O, rn/m) se diferencian a propósito. El Braille
Institute la publicó bajo la SIL Open Font Licence 1.1, que permite
usarla y redistribuirla libremente.

El Inclusive Design Research Centre de la Universidad OCAD documenta
Atkinson Hyperlegible como tipo de letra recomendado para la
accesibilidad en casos de baja visión.

## Soberanía y rendimiento

Ninguna de las dos opciones tipográficas carga fuentes desde Google
Fonts ni desde ninguna otra fuente externa. No hay conexión con una
red de distribución de fuentes de terceros ni se revelan las
direcciones IP de los visitantes a proveedores de fuentes.

Cuando system-ui está activa, el texto aparece de inmediato con una
fuente que ya está en el dispositivo: sin solicitud de red, sin
destello de texto invisible y sin saltos en la maquetación.
""")

page("recursos/guia-auditoria-infraestructura.md", {
    "title": "Guía de auditoría de infraestructura — Mapear lo que tiene antes de cambiarlo",
    "navTitle": "Guía de auditoría de infraestructura", "order": 2,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:b11022df-d208-4fb2-9f19-27e4677cab01",
    "description": "Una guía práctica para hacer una auditoría completa de infraestructura: qué documentar, cómo sacar a la luz las dependencias ocultas y cómo producir un mapa que de verdad sirva para tomar decisiones.",
}, """
Una guía práctica para hacer una auditoría completa de infraestructura:
qué documentar, cómo sacar a la luz las dependencias ocultas y cómo
producir un mapa que de verdad sirva para tomar decisiones.

## Propósito

Antes de empezar cualquier trabajo de infraestructura, necesita una
imagen precisa de lo que existe. Esta guía describe cómo hacer una
auditoría completa de infraestructura: no un inventario teórico, sino
un documento de trabajo que refleje el sistema tal como funciona en
realidad.

## Qué registrar

Una auditoría de infraestructura útil registra seis categorías de
información:

- **Servicios**: cada servicio en funcionamiento, su propósito, quién lo opera y de qué depende
- **Flujos de datos**: dónde se originan los datos, dónde se procesan, dónde se almacenan y dónde salen de su control
- **Accesos y credenciales**: quién tiene acceso a qué, con qué modelo de autenticación y dónde se guardan las credenciales
- **Dependencias externas**: cada servicio, API o plataforma de terceros de la que depende el sistema
- **Contratos y costos**: cada contrato con proveedores, su fecha de renovación, su costo y lo que costaría salir de él
- **Documentación**: qué documentación existe, qué tan actualizada está y dónde se encuentra

## Cómo sacar a la luz las dependencias ocultas

Las dependencias ocultas son la parte más peligrosa de cualquier
infraestructura. Son cosas de las que el sistema depende sin que nadie
haya decidido explícitamente depender de ellas, acumuladas a lo largo
de años de decisiones prácticas que nunca se revisaron.

Algunas fuentes comunes de dependencias ocultas:

- Registros DNS que apuntan a servicios que ya no existen, pero cuya eliminación rompería algo
- Envío de correo que depende de una cuenta personal de una persona que ya no trabaja en la organización
- Flujos de autenticación que pasan por un servicio de terceros añadido hace años como medida temporal
- Tareas de copia de seguridad que escriben en un lugar que se quedó sin espacio sin que nadie se diera cuenta
- Certificados SSL gestionados por una persona que dejó la organización

La forma más fiable de sacar a la luz las dependencias ocultas es
mapear los flujos de datos de afuera hacia adentro: partir de cada URL
pública y seguir cada solicitud a través del sistema hasta que llegue a
un almacenamiento persistente o salga hacia un tercero.

## Producir un mapa útil

Un mapa de infraestructura solo es útil si refleja el sistema real y si
lo puede leer alguien que no lo construyó. Debe incluir:

- Un diagrama con los componentes principales y las conexiones entre ellos
- Una tabla de servicios con responsable, dependencias y fecha de la última verificación
- Una lista de dependencias externas con información de contratos y costos
- Una lista de preguntas abiertas que la auditoría planteó pero no pudo resolver

El mapa debe estar bajo control de versiones junto con la
infraestructura que describe, y actualizarse cada vez que se haga un
cambio importante.
""")

page("recursos/lista-verificacion-accesibilidad.md", {
    "title": "Lista de verificación de accesibilidad para adquisiciones — Qué preguntar antes de comprar",
    "navTitle": "Lista de verificación de accesibilidad", "order": 3,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:5ac1ea1b-9000-4cbb-9a6d-ac7749fc7625",
    "description": "Una lista de verificación para evaluar lo que se afirma sobre accesibilidad al adquirir software: revisión del VPAT, pruebas independientes, compromisos contractuales y qué hacer cuando un proveedor no puede responder sus preguntas.",
}, """
Una lista de verificación para evaluar lo que se afirma sobre
accesibilidad al adquirir software: revisión del VPAT, pruebas
independientes, compromisos contractuales y qué hacer cuando un
proveedor no puede responder sus preguntas.

## Propósito

La mayoría de los proveedores de software le dirán que su producto es
accesible. Esta lista le ayuda a evaluar esa afirmación antes de firmar
un contrato, y no después de haberse comprometido con una plataforma
que sus usuarios no pueden usar.

## Pida el VPAT

Un VPAT (Voluntary Product Accessibility Template) es la evaluación que
hace el propio proveedor de cómo su producto cumple las normas de
accesibilidad. Pida el VPAT de la versión exacta del producto que está
evaluando, con respecto al nivel AA de las WCAG 2.2.

Señales de alerta en un VPAT:

- Hace referencia a las WCAG 2.0 o 2.1 en lugar de las 2.2
- Todos los criterios figuran como «Compatible» sin ninguna explicación
- La evaluación la hizo el propio proveedor, sin revisión independiente
- Corresponde a una versión del producto con más de una versión mayor de antigüedad

## Haga pruebas independientes

No se fíe solo del VPAT. Haga o encargue pruebas independientes antes
de comprar. Como mínimo:

- Ejecute un análisis automático con una herramienta actual (Axe, WAVE u otra equivalente)
- Recorra los flujos principales usando solo el teclado
- Pruebe con un lector de pantalla (NVDA en Windows, VoiceOver en macOS e iOS)
- Verifique el contraste de color de todo el texto y de los elementos interactivos

## Haga preguntas contractuales

Antes de firmar, pregunte:

- ¿Cuál es el objetivo de conformidad de accesibilidad que publica el proveedor?
- ¿Cuál es el proceso para informar problemas de accesibilidad?
- ¿En qué plazo se compromete a corregir las barreras de accesibilidad críticas?
- ¿Los compromisos de accesibilidad están incluidos en el acuerdo de nivel de servicio?

Un proveedor que no puede responder estas preguntas es un proveedor
que no ha hecho de la accesibilidad una prioridad. Esa es información
útil.

## Cuando un proveedor no puede cumplir sus requisitos

Si un proveedor no puede demostrar la conformidad y no acepta
compromisos contractuales, usted tiene tres opciones: exigir la
conformidad como condición del contrato, exigir un plan de corrección
con hitos como condición del contrato o elegir otro proveedor.

Aceptar un producto inaccesible porque cumple otros requisitos es una
decisión que excluye a una parte de sus usuarios. Esa decisión debe
tomarse de forma explícita y quedar documentada, no diluirse en
silencio dentro de un proceso de adquisición.
""")

page("recursos/marco-autoalojamiento.md", {
    "title": "Marco de decisión sobre autoalojamiento — Cuándo operarlo usted mismo y cuándo no",
    "navTitle": "Marco de decisión sobre autoalojamiento", "order": 4,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:2428f521-d6fb-4493-9b62-e569e02ba7ab",
    "description": "Un marco práctico para decidir cuándo autoalojar un servicio mejora la capacidad de acción de su organización y cuándo introduce complejidad sin un beneficio proporcional.",
}, """
Un marco práctico para decidir cuándo autoalojar un servicio mejora la
capacidad de acción de su organización y cuándo introduce complejidad
sin un beneficio proporcional.

## Propósito

Autoalojar no es intrínsecamente mejor que usar un servicio gestionado.
La pregunta siempre es si autoalojar este servicio, en esta
organización y en este momento, da un mejor resultado que las
alternativas disponibles. Este marco ayuda a estructurar esa decisión.

## Las cuatro preguntas

Antes de decidir autoalojar cualquier servicio, responda cuatro
preguntas:

1. **¿Qué gana?** Enumere los beneficios concretos: soberanía de los
   datos, menor costo, eliminación de una dependencia de un proveedor,
   coherencia con un compromiso de privacidad, la posibilidad de
   adaptar un comportamiento que el proveedor no admite. Sea concreto.
   «Más control» no basta: ¿control sobre qué, exactamente?
2. **¿Cuánto cuesta operarlo?** Los servicios autoalojados necesitan a
   alguien que los mantenga: que aplique las actualizaciones de
   seguridad, vigile las fallas, gestione las copias de seguridad y
   responda cuando algo se rompe. ¿Quién lo hará? ¿Qué capacidad
   tiene? ¿Qué pasa cuando esa persona no está disponible?
3. **¿Cómo falla?** Si el servicio autoalojado falla, ¿cuál es el
   impacto? ¿Qué tan rápido se puede restablecer? ¿Hay un procedimiento
   de recuperación probado? Cuando falla un servicio autoalojado,
   normalmente le toca a usted resolverlo, algo que no ocurre de la
   misma manera con un servicio gestionado.
4. **¿Cuánto cuesta salir?** Si autoalojar resulta ser la decisión
   equivocada, ¿cuánto esfuerzo cuesta migrar a un servicio
   gestionado? Un costo de salida bajo hace que la decisión sea
   reversible. Un costo de salida alto significa que necesita más
   seguridad antes de comprometerse.

## Cuándo autoalojar es claramente lo correcto

Autoalojar es claramente lo correcto cuando:

- Los datos que procesa el servicio son sensibles y están sujetos a requisitos de jurisdicción que los servicios gestionados no pueden cumplir
- La organización tiene la capacidad operativa para mantener el servicio de forma fiable
- Las alternativas gestionadas son demasiado caras en relación con el valor que aportan
- Las alternativas gestionadas crean una dependencia inaceptable

## Cuándo un servicio gestionado es claramente lo correcto

Un servicio gestionado es claramente lo correcto cuando:

- El costo operativo de autoalojar supera el costo del servicio gestionado
- La organización no tiene la capacidad de responder a las fallas de forma fiable
- El servicio no forma parte de las competencias operativas centrales de la organización
- Los datos procesados no son sensibles y la jurisdicción no es un problema

## La respuesta honesta, la mayoría de las veces

La mayoría de las organizaciones deberían autoalojar menos cosas de las
que defienden los idealistas y más de las que prefieren los
proveedores. La respuesta correcta depende por completo de la capacidad
operativa, de la sensibilidad de los datos y de las alternativas
concretas disponibles. Quien le dé una respuesta general no está
teniendo en cuenta su situación real.
""")

page("recursos/introduccion-tokens-diseno.md", {
    "title": "Introducción a los tokens de diseño — Lo mínimo que necesita saber",
    "navTitle": "Tokens de diseño", "order": 5,
    "relation": "urn:uuid:7e63069a-95ae-4170-b805-603e14d4de76",
    "description": "Una introducción en lenguaje claro a los tokens de diseño: qué son, por qué importan para el diseño multilingüe y accesible, y cómo implementar un sistema mínimo de tokens sin suscribirse a una herramienta de diseño.",
}, """
Una introducción en lenguaje claro a los tokens de diseño: qué son, por
qué importan para el diseño multilingüe y accesible, y cómo implementar
un sistema mínimo de tokens sin suscribirse a una herramienta de
diseño.

## ¿Qué es un token de diseño?

Un token de diseño es un valor con nombre que representa una decisión
de diseño. En lugar de escribir `color: #0033cc` en quinientos lugares,
se define un token, `--colour-primary: #0033cc`, y se usa ese token en
todas partes. Cuando la decisión cambia, se cambia en un solo lugar.

Los tokens son la capa de infraestructura de un sistema de diseño. No
son una función de una herramienta de diseño ni un requisito de un
framework. Son propiedades personalizadas de CSS y funcionan en
cualquier navegador.

## Por qué los tokens importan para un diseño accesible y multilingüe

**Accesibilidad**: los tokens permiten verificar el contraste de color
de todo un sistema. Si el color del texto y el color del fondo son
tokens, puede revisar todas las combinaciones en un solo lugar, en
lugar de buscar valores escritos a mano por todo el código.

**Diseño multilingüe**: los tokens facilitan ajustar las decisiones
tipográficas para idiomas específicos. Una interfaz en francés o en
español puede necesitar un interlineado un poco más generoso que una
en inglés. Un sistema basado en tokens le permite cambiar un solo valor
por idioma en lugar de reescribir las reglas de maquetación.

**Mantenimiento**: un equipo pequeño puede mantener un sistema basado
en tokens porque los cambios están localizados. Reemplazar el color
principal lleva dos minutos, no dos días.

## Un sistema mínimo de tokens

Un sistema mínimo de tokens para una organización pequeña suele
necesitar cuatro categorías:

- **Color**: de tres a cinco colores como máximo. Un color principal, un color de texto, un color de fondo, un color de borde y un color semántico (para errores o advertencias, si hace falta). Cualquier otro color del sistema debe derivarse de estos o ser blanco o negro.
- **Tipografía**: dos o tres tamaños de letra para el texto, uno o dos para los títulos y uno para las etiquetas pequeñas. Un interlineado para cada uno. Una pila de fuentes por cada tipo de letra que se use.
- **Espaciado**: de cuatro a seis valores de espaciado en una escala coherente, por ejemplo 0.25rem, 0.5rem, 1rem, 2rem, 4rem. Todo lo demás se compone a partir de estos.
- **Maquetación**: un ancho máximo para el contenido y un valor de separación estándar para las cuadrículas.

## Implementación

```css
:root {
  --colour-primary: #0033cc;
  --colour-text: #000000;
  --colour-background: #ffffff;
  --colour-border: #d0d0d0;
  --font-body: system-ui, sans-serif;
  --size-sm: 0.875rem;
  --size-base: 1rem;
  --size-lg: 1.25rem;
  --size-xl: 1.75rem;
  --space-sm: 0.5rem;
  --space-md: 1rem;
  --space-lg: 2rem;
  --space-xl: 4rem;
  --measure: 70ch;
}
```

Ese es un sistema mínimo de tokens completo. Todo lo demás es
composición.
""")
